Sutra Full Audit
Audit Scope
This audit covers the current main snapshot at commit 0b25a8906604721dad3798d2db0e01b2249d1884, committed at 11:03 p.m. EDT on August 23, 2026. The repository, source files, architecture documents, workflows, tests, production shell, live product structure, persistence systems, sync implementation, representative feature modules, responsive systems, and security boundaries were inspected in read-only mode. No repository files, branches, commits, issues, or settings were changed.
The test suite was not executed during this connector-based audit, so the testing assessment evaluates test design and coverage, not whether every test currently passes. The UI assessment is based on the live product structure, HTML, CSS, interaction code, responsive behavior, and tests; it is not a pixel-by-pixel computer-use review, so the UI score has somewhat lower confidence than the engineering scores.
The separately attached launch-video reference note was not treated as codebase evidence.
Executive Summary
Sutra is simultaneously more production-minded and less maintainable than it first appears.
It is not a toy. Its encrypted synchronization, recovery system, backup handling, locked-note boundaries, migration discipline, offline support, deployment pipeline, and adversarial tests are substantially more serious than those found in most single-developer browser applications.
The problem is that these production-grade safety systems surround a prototype-derived application kernel that has grown far beyond its original architectural capacity. The central src/core/app.js file is approximately 4.85 MB, with the repository itself describing it as a roughly 64,000-line global runtime. Most newer modules remain classic scripts connected through mutable window APIs, DOM events, observers, polling, and load-order assumptions.
The result is not uniformly bad engineering. It is good subsystem engineering inside a strained whole-system architecture.
Sutra’s largest strength is its seriousness about protecting student data. Its largest weakness is that too many unrelated responsibilities still converge inside one runtime, one global namespace, one cascade, and one persistence bridge. The architecture can still support Sutra today, but it is already making ordinary changes more expensive and dangerous than they should be.
Approximate Ratings
Area
	Rating
	Assessment
	
Engineering / Codebase
	6.5 / 10
	Many individual modules are careful and robust, but the central runtime and global coupling reduce the overall score.
	
Architecture
	4.5 / 10
	The local-first architecture remains sound; the internal application architecture is at its scaling limit.
	
Reliability
	7.5 / 10
	Strong root persistence, recovery, migrations, backup, and sync. A few mutation paths do not fully honor their advertised durability contracts.
	
Maintainability
	4.0 / 10
	Large global kernel, load-order dependencies, duplicate implementations, CSS precedence dependencies, and bridge-based coupling.
	
UI
	6.5 / 10
	Strong design intent, tokens, responsive contracts, and polished core surfaces. Consistency is weakened by accumulated feature layers and bespoke UI.
	
UX
	6.5 / 10
	The student daily loop is coherent; advanced feature breadth, terminology drift, and multiple overlapping concepts increase cognitive load.
	
Performance
	4.5 / 10
	Offline capability is strong, but initial parsing, eager loading, whole-workspace operations, polling, and oversized critical caches present substantial risk.
	
Testing
	8.0 / 10
	Unusually broad and meaningful coverage, especially around sync and data safety. Accessibility and some contract tests provide less confidence than their names imply.
	
Security / Privacy Engineering
	7.0 / 10
	Excellent encryption and privacy intent, weakened by permissive CSP, deployment-header ambiguity, same-origin credential limitations, and one latent assistant privacy defect.
	
Overall Product Coherence
	6.5 / 10
	Today, Notes, Homework, Timeline, Review, and Focus form a coherent core. Several peripheral tools feel added faster than they have been consolidated.
	
Overall assessment: approximately 6.3 / 10.
That score should not be read as “mediocre software.” Sutra has several 9/10 subsystems and several 3/10 structural foundations. Its quality is highly uneven.
What Is GOOD
1. The local-first product and data model
Sutra’s most important architectural decision remains correct: the browser workspace is authoritative, an account is not required, network use is optional, and the core product remains usable without a backend. That aligns the implementation with the product’s privacy promise rather than treating privacy as marketing copy.
The manifest, shell, onboarding, and public product story consistently position Sutra as an installable student workspace whose notes, assignments, planning, and review data remain in the browser by default. Optional Assistant and Sync capabilities are presented as separate decisions. (tanujranjith.github.io)
This should be preserved. Moving the primary workspace into a required remote backend would simplify some engineering problems but would weaken Sutra’s product differentiation and threat model.
2. Sutra Sync is the strongest subsystem
Sutra Sync is closer to production-grade infrastructure than any other major subsystem.
It includes:
AES-GCM payload encryption with authenticated metadata.

A high-work-factor passphrase derivation path.

Wrapped workspace keys and recovery material.

Deterministic record projection.

Durable outbox operations.

Idempotent operation identifiers.

Lamport-style ordering.

Tombstones and deletion retention.

Stale-cursor handling and retries.

Conflict persistence before applying the merged workspace.

Device and account isolation.

Asset completeness handling.

Supabase row-level security and RPC-based ownership enforcement.

Fail-closed behavior when state is inconsistent.

The backend schema does not trust client-supplied ownership fields, and the client does not treat the server as the plaintext source of truth. The synchronization service can observe metadata such as record types, device IDs, sizes, hashes, timing, and cursor activity, but it cannot read encrypted payload content. That is an appropriate and clearly bounded tradeoff for this architecture.
This system should be evolved, not rewritten. Its deterministic protocol, projection model, and explicit conflict handling are worth preserving.
3. Persistence and recovery receive serious engineering attention
The canonical workspace database has transactional writes, backup records, commit markers, conflict-aware writes, connection lifecycle handling, and retry behavior. The latest persistence work also performs canonical hashing and readback verification to distinguish real stale-tab conflicts from inconsequential representation differences.
The surrounding failure systems are particularly good:
Startup health checks distinguish a slow startup from a genuinely missing critical subsystem.

Safe Mode pauses optional systems while keeping Notes, persistence, backup, and diagnostics available.

Emergency backup remains accessible during degraded operation.

Storage hygiene uses review-first deletion with freshness and state-change checks.

Legacy migration stages and verifies data before clearing old storage.

Import paths normalize and validate before applying changes.

This demonstrates a correct priority: when Sutra fails, it should fail in a way that protects the student’s work.
4. The release pipeline tests the artifact that is actually deployed
The deploy workflow rebuilds the static artifact once, validates it, runs the browser suite against that exact artifact, uploads that same artifact to GitHub Pages, and then runs a live smoke check. This avoids a common release error where tests run against source or one build while production receives another.
The workflow also runs the full Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, responsive, and device matrix before production deployment. Action dependencies are pinned by commit rather than floating tags.
This is excellent release discipline. It is substantially better than relying on local manual testing.
5. The test suite addresses real failure modes
The strongest tests are not merely selector checks. The repository contains meaningful tests for:
Sync encryption and merge behavior.

Stale cursors and outbox recovery.

Conflicts and partial failures.

Account and device isolation.

Storage failures.

Migration round trips.

Encrypted backups.

Locked-note privacy.

Hostile or malformed DOM input.

Import normalization.

Property-style and fuzz scenarios.

Multi-browser behavior.

Mobile navigation.

Recovery mode.

The locked-note privacy test is particularly strong. It verifies that a locked note’s plaintext cannot escape through the editor, search, review generation, backlinks, Canvas linked-note cards, Slides, or assistant-facing context. That is the right way to test a privacy property: across every secondary surface that could accidentally bypass the main lock UI.
6. Plugin isolation is well designed
The experimental plugin system uses sandboxed iframes, omits same-origin privileges, applies an internal network-restrictive CSP, validates operations and tokens, limits plugin size, and routes changes through reviewable permissions. Custom CSS is treated as an explicit host-level customization risk rather than silently mixed with executable plugin code.
This is a thoughtful design. A locally installed plugin system could easily have become arbitrary same-origin code execution. Sutra avoids that.
7. Mobile navigation is a true adaptation
The mobile experience is not simply the desktop shell at a smaller width.
The mobile navigation derives from canonical route definitions, presents a constrained five-slot dock, moves secondary routes into an “All sections” sheet, handles browser history, traps focus in overlays, restores focus, respects safe-area insets, supports reduced motion, and gives Notes its own contextual tree behavior.
The decision to hide the Notes hierarchy outside Notes is also correct. It preserves space and prevents a note-specific navigation structure from appearing to control unrelated areas.
8. The newer design contracts are good
The semantic token layer establishes consistent spacing, typography, control sizing, colors, motion, safe areas, and a documented z-index ladder. The interaction contract establishes global focus visibility, disabled states, touch-target minimums, modal layering, reduced-motion behavior, and mobile bottom-nav spacing.
These files represent the right direction. They should become more authoritative over time.
9. Several extracted modules demonstrate the correct decomposition pattern
The workspace entity registry is a good example. It provides one contract for finding, opening, searching, and acting on heterogeneous records without taking ownership of their canonical stores. It also normalizes privacy, strips sensitive metadata, catches adapter failures, and exposes explicit invalidation.
The import engine follows a similarly good pattern: parse, bound, normalize, identify provenance, preview, deduplicate, and only then allow application. The Notes Editor v2 also preserves the existing storage format while replacing the editing model, which avoids a dangerous simultaneous editor and data-format migration.
These are the patterns future extraction work should copy.
What Is MID
1. The canonical workspace object is useful, but increasingly expensive
Keeping one portable workspace root gives Sutra simple backups, predictable imports, deterministic sync projection, and a single conceptual source of truth. That is valuable.
However, much of the runtime maintains live variables outside appData, then serializes those bindings back into appData before saving. Editors may also maintain their own internal state and mirror it into legacy DOM elements. This means Sutra has one persisted root but several temporary sources of truth while the application is running.
Consequences include:
Larger save and hash operations as the workspace grows.

Risk of stale live bindings overwriting newly imported or synchronized values.

Complicated hydration guards.

More difficult transactional reasoning across features.

Increased dependence on precise lifecycle ordering.

This needs incremental cleanup, not an immediate normalized-database redesign.
2. Modularization has started, but most boundaries are organizational
The repository has a sensible folder map and many extracted modules, but most still load as classic scripts into the same global environment. The first state extraction explicitly says it remains in the same shared global scope so old call sites continue working.
This is a sensible migration strategy, but it should not be confused with completed modularity. Dependency direction is not enforced, private state is often not private, and a module can still reach across the application through globals or the DOM.
The current state is MID because the migration direction is correct, but the boundaries do not yet provide the maintenance benefits expected from modules.
3. The CSS system is halfway through a successful migration
The repository is candid that CSS precedence is load-order dependent, mobile CSS must remain late, and six legacy stylesheets still use !important and must not grow. Approximately 2,900 lines of legacy inline shell CSS were externalized without changing behavior.
That is worthwhile progress, but folders are currently an organizational map, not an encapsulation system. Many components can still be affected by distant selectors, theme overrides, late mobile rules, or legacy !important declarations.
This can be improved incrementally by increasing component ownership and shrinking legacy layers.
4. Accessibility intent is stronger than accessibility enforcement
There is real accessibility work:
Central modal focus management.

Escape handling.

Focus restoration.

inert and aria-hidden.

Global focus-visible styles.

Coarse-pointer target sizing.

Reduced-motion support.

Navigation keyboard tests.

Accessible labels in many generated controls.

However, the general accessibility suite contains assertions such as counts being greater than or equal to zero, logs some violations instead of failing, and samples only the first subset of elements. This can make the suite appear more comprehensive than it is.
Accessibility is not absent. It is inconsistently enforced.
5. The optional feature registry is not yet a real isolation boundary
The registry can load declared scripts and styles, invoke initialization, and expose feature state. That is useful for progressive delivery.
Its weaknesses include:
Failed asset promises are cached without a clear retry lifecycle.

Script assets cannot be unloaded.

No dependency-cycle detection.

No transactional rollback when initialization partially succeeds.

State can become enabled before all initialization consequences complete.

Large feature packs still communicate through globals.

The current manifest covers only a small fraction of Sutra’s actual surface area.

It is a loader and organizational seam, not a plugin-quality module system.
6. The new document editors are ambitious but uneven
The Notes Editor v2 has a careful compatibility strategy and a real document model. Slides and Sheets are much more prototype-like.
Sheets does virtualize visible cells, which is correct. However, each scroll reconstructs row and column offsets for at least 10,000 rows and 100 columns, reevaluates the workbook, and rebuilds visible DOM. It also uses browser prompts for several advanced operations, which is functional but not polished.
Slides has capable local editing, import/export, object manipulation, history, and locked-page checks. It also contains duplicate top-level mount() and mutate() implementations, with later declarations overriding earlier ones, and it polls for page changes every 350 milliseconds. Sheets performs similar polling every 400 milliseconds.
These tools work, but they have not yet reached the same engineering maturity as Sync, recovery, or the newer Notes editor.
7. Product breadth is both a strength and a coherence problem
The core workflow is coherent:
Today → Homework → Notes → Timeline → Focus → Review
Beyond that core, Sutra also contains Courses, Testing Hub, AP Study, Cram Hub, College applications, broader College planning, Life, wellness, spending, nutrition, sleep, Business, Canvas, Slides, Sheets, HTML pages, PDF workspaces, plugins, extensive themes, cloud backup, Sync, and multiple Assistant modes.
Feature packs and progressive disclosure help, but the peripheral product increasingly risks feeling like a collection of applications sharing one shell. The public product story remains clear, yet the live interface exposes a much larger conceptual footprint. (tanujranjith.github.io) (Tanuj Ranjith)
8. First-time vocabulary is not fully canonical
The public product and normal navigation use Today and Notes, while parts of setup use Home and Create. Setup also asks users to enable broad destination categories while some core default routes are enabled implicitly. (tanujranjith.github.io) (tanujranjith.github.io)
This is not a cosmetic issue. Navigation names teach the product’s mental model. First-time users should not have to infer that Home means Today or Create means Notes and its embedded document modes.
9. The credential vault is useful, but its threat model needs precise wording
Remembered provider credentials are protected with a non-exportable AES key stored in IndexedDB and bound to the origin. Session-only credentials remain the default. This is substantially better than storing plaintext API keys in localStorage.
However, an origin-bound key does not protect credentials from malicious JavaScript already executing within Sutra’s origin. Such code can ask the browser to decrypt credentials even if it cannot export the key. The vault protects against casual storage inspection and some local extraction scenarios; it is not a defense against same-origin XSS.
10. Vendoring improves offline behavior but complicates dependency governance
Sutra has only one ordinary runtime package dependency, but that understates the real dependency footprint. Editor, PDF, worker, font, math, highlighting, and Office interoperability runtimes are vendored directly.
This is good for deterministic offline behavior. It also means conventional dependency scanners will not automatically identify every vulnerable vendored asset. Sutra’s version checks help, but the project needs a first-class vendored dependency inventory and update policy.
What Is BAD
No confirmed finding reached Critical severity. The following findings are ranked by expected impact.
1. The central global runtime is structurally oversized
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic
src/core/app.js is 4,851,661 bytes and is described by the repository as a roughly 64,000-line global runtime. It owns or coordinates application state, hydration, persistence, import/export, Notes, navigation, settings, numerous views, sync bridges, modal systems, and compatibility behavior.
This creates several problems:
A developer cannot understand one behavior by reading one module.

Private helper dependencies make extraction dangerous.

Global variable names become implicit APIs.

Changes have a large regression radius.

Testing requires extensive browser fixtures because pure unit boundaries are limited.

Load order becomes part of the architecture.

Dead or duplicate code is difficult to identify safely.

The central file becomes a merge-conflict and review bottleneck.

The repository’s guardrail baseline also accepts hundreds of raw HTML sinks, direct storage accesses, and a large global export inventory as existing debt. The ratchet prevents additional deterioration, but it does not make the inherited surface safe or maintainable.
This is the largest engineering weakness in Sutra.
2. The intended security-header configuration does not match the production deployment path
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic deployment/security boundary
The HTML includes a meta CSP, but it permits 'unsafe-inline' for scripts and styles and allows a broad set of third-party script, connection, and frame destinations. That considerably reduces CSP’s value as an XSS containment mechanism.
The stronger response-header policy is defined in vercel.json, including frame restrictions, nosniff, referrer policy, permissions policy, HSTS, COOP, and CORP. Production, however, is deployed through the GitHub Pages workflow. The deployment workflow does not consume vercel.json.
The repository’s standard header check validates the intended Vercel configuration rather than proving what the GitHub Pages deployment actually sends. The live smoke test checks routes, assets, startup requests, and console failures, but not the complete response-header policy.
This matters because Sutra stores sensitive local data and optionally remembered credentials in the same origin. A script injection has unusually high impact.
3. Homework’s “durable” persistence contract is not wired durably
Severity: High
Scope: Localized subsystem with architectural implications
The canonical Homework store is well designed in isolation. It has synchronous and durable mutation paths, serializes durable operations, and can roll back state when an awaited persistence adapter fails.
The application adapter defeats that guarantee:
persist: () => queueMicrotask(() => {
    try { persistAppData(); }
    catch (...) { ... }
})The adapter returns immediately. Therefore:
commitDurably() has no real persistence promise to await.

Its rollback cannot respond to a later IndexedDB failure.

The surrounding try/catch observes only synchronous scheduling errors.

The main Homework UI uses the synchronous replacement path and reports the mutation before durability is known.

Sutra’s separate persistence-health system may eventually surface a save failure, so this is not guaranteed silent data loss. It is still a mismatch between the domain contract and the actual adapter semantics.
4. Startup and runtime loading strategy is too expensive for the product’s breadth
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic performance risk
Sutra loads a long parser-ordered chain of scripts around the central runtime. Many large features are loaded eagerly even when the student never uses them, including the optional Editor v2 bundle, Canvas tooling, customization, academic planning, PDF infrastructure, Slides, Sheets, and other advanced surfaces.
The service worker treats the PDF stack, workers, fonts, and hundreds of mapping assets as critical installation resources. That gives Sutra impressive offline PDF capability, but it makes fresh installation and cache rotation large and failure-sensitive.
Additional runtime costs include:
Slides polling every 350 ms.

Sheets polling every 400 ms.

Sheets recalculating large offset arrays and workbook evaluation during scrolling.

Whole-workspace serialization and hashing.

Large global CSS layers.

No performance budget in the normal verification pipeline.

This is primarily an architectural performance risk rather than proof that every current device is slow. It will become more visible on lower-powered phones and larger student workspaces.
5. Route and presentation ownership is fragmented
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic UI architecture
primary-nav-visibility.js observes DOM changes from other navigation systems, writes inline !important styles, and schedules reconciliation after 0, 100, 500, 1,000, and 2,000 milliseconds. That is a compatibility repair, not a stable state model.
Similar patterns appear through:
Mutation observers.

Custom events.

Polling loops.

Late CSS overrides.

DOM inspection to infer current state.

Multiple modules reacting to the same route.

State repair after initialization instead of deterministic composition.

This makes navigation sensitive to timing and feature load order. It also explains why UI fixes can require several additional “repair” modules rather than one change to the route owner.
6. SutraFeatureGuard does not isolate asynchronous failures as advertised
Severity: Medium
Scope: Localized core utility
For a promise-returning feature, run() attaches a rejection handler but returns the original rejecting promise. The feature is marked degraded, but the caller still receives a rejection and an ignored caller can still produce an unhandled rejection.
When opts.rethrow is enabled, the attached rejection handler throws inside a detached promise branch, which can create another unhandled rejection.
The comment says asynchronous functions are caught and degraded like synchronous functions. The implementation observes them but does not convert them to the configured fallback contract.
7. Accessibility tests can create false confidence
Severity: Medium
Scope: Systemic testing gap
Several accessibility assertions cannot fail meaningfully, some violations are printed instead of asserted, and only subsets of controls are sampled. The modal-specific tests are stronger, but the broad suite does not guarantee that all controls have names, minimum target sizes, valid roles, or keyboard-operable behavior.
For a product with this many custom controls, editors, dialogs, drawers, tabs, and mobile gestures, accessibility cannot rely primarily on convention.
8. The assistant private-document policy has a latent deny-by-default defect
Severity: Medium
Scope: Localized privacy boundary
assistant-permissions.js states that private documents are excluded by default and includes allowPrivateDocuments in its permission model. However, privateDocuments is not mapped to a protected context area, and the sensitive-field removal operates on the field’s value rather than removing the top-level field itself.
The existing unit test verifies that the access report says private documents were excluded, but it never supplies a privateDocuments field, so it misses the defect.
The current assistant context builder does not add private documents to its bounded context, so no current exfiltration path was confirmed. The defect remains important because the policy helper fails its advertised contract if a future context builder includes that field. The outbound provider boundary should enforce deny-by-default independently of caller behavior.
9. main is unprotected even though pushes deploy production
Severity: Medium
Scope: Repository governance
The main branch reports protected: false, with no required status checks. The current commit is also unsigned. A direct push to main initiates the deployment pipeline.
The deploy workflow itself is strong, but repository policy should prevent bypassing review and required checks. A strong pipeline is not equivalent to protected release governance.
10. Duplicate and dead implementations remain in live feature files
Severity: Medium
Scope: Recurring feature-level smell
slides.js contains duplicate top-level implementations of mount() and mutate(). JavaScript function hoisting causes the later versions to replace the earlier versions, leaving the older implementations dead but still parsed, reviewed, and potentially modified by mistake.
This is concrete evidence that some features have been extended by appending replacements rather than removing superseded implementations. It increases bundle size, cognitive load, and regression risk.
Architecture Assessment
The architecture Sutra actually has
Sutra is best described as a static local-first monolith with an extracted module halo.
1. Static shell
Sutra.html establishes the page structure and loads styles and classic scripts in a carefully controlled order. There is no bundler or framework runtime.
2. Global application kernel
src/core/app.js owns the canonical in-memory workspace and most lifecycle behavior. It also exposes bridges and test hooks that allow other scripts to reach internal capabilities.
3. Extracted global modules
Core safety, domain logic, feature engines, persistence, Sync, UI helpers, and optional packs are separated into files, but most attach themselves to window and communicate through:
Shared globals.

flowAtelier and similar bridges.

Custom DOM events.

Direct DOM queries.

Mutation observers.

Timers and polling.

Callbacks supplied by the kernel.

4. Canonical persistence plus separate binary storage
Most structured state is persisted as one workspace root in IndexedDB. Large attachments and related bytes are stored separately. This preserves portable backups and avoids placing every blob inside the root object.
5. Projection-based synchronization
The root workspace is projected into deterministic per-record encrypted operations for Sutra Sync, then reassembled through merge rules.
6. CSS cascade layers
The styling architecture consists of a large base sheet, feature/theme layers, late responsive overrides, and legacy sheets whose relative link position is behaviorally significant.
What has scaled well
The following architectural decisions have scaled:
Static deployment.

Local-first authority.

Portable workspace backups.

Separate attachment storage.

Deterministic Sync projection.

Optional remote services.

Review-before-apply imports and AI actions.

Feature packs as product-level progressive disclosure.

Compatibility-preserving migrations.

What is starting to strain
The application kernel, not the local-first model, is failing to scale.
The most strained areas are:
Global mutable runtime state.

Lifecycle ordering.

Navigation ownership.

Persistence bridge semantics.

Editor mirrors.

CSS precedence.

Eager script loading.

Cross-feature DOM repair.

Duplicate compatibility implementations.

The number of concepts exposed through one shell.

The correct response is not a wholesale rewrite. The correct response is a staged transfer of ownership from app.js and DOM-observed state into explicit services and stores.
Code Quality Assessment
Strong aspects
Individual modules often show excellent defensive habits:
Bounded input sizes.

Explicit normalization.

Stable identifiers.

Quarantine of malformed data.

Unknown-field preservation.

Idempotent operations.

Defensive cloning.

Clear comments describing invariants.

Fallback behavior when optional systems fail.

Structured error reporting.

Explicit privacy metadata.

Reviewable operations.

Sync, import, storage hygiene, recovery, workspace entity registry, and the newer Notes editor are particularly strong examples.
Weak aspects
At whole-codebase level, maintainability is poor.
Global names are implicit APIs
A large number of window.* exports serve as cross-module dependencies. There is no compiler or module linker enforcing ownership, type compatibility, or dependency direction.
Files are frequently too large
The central runtime is the clearest example, but several feature modules also combine model normalization, rendering, event handling, import/export, persistence, keyboard handling, and application integration.
Duplicate logic remains active in source
Slides demonstrates literal duplicate function implementations. Similar compatibility layers appear elsewhere through old and new naming, mirrors, adapters, and post-load repair scripts.
Naming carries historical residue
Atelier, Flow, NoteFlow, cw, hw, and newer Sutra terminology coexist. This is understandable during migration, but it increases onboarding cost for another engineer and makes code search less reliable.
No static type system protects contracts
Runtime normalization is strong, but bridge objects, event payloads, global APIs, and persistence adapters are structurally typed only by convention. Many current bugs are contract mismatches that a typed interface could have exposed.
Comments sometimes compensate for architecture
The code is often exceptionally well commented. That is positive. In several areas, however, the comments explain why a complicated load order, mirror, compatibility path, or repair loop must exist. Good documentation reduces danger but does not eliminate the underlying coupling.
Reliability / Data Integrity Assessment
Production-grade elements
Sutra’s core data-protection posture is strong:
Local workspace authority.

IndexedDB persistence.

Transactional root writes.

Backup and commit markers.

Readback verification.

Stale-tab conflict checks.

Multi-tab coordination.

Recovery mode.

Emergency export.

Migration history.

Unknown-field preservation.

Encrypted portable backup.

Sync conflict persistence.

Attachment completeness gates.

Locked-content authorization checks.

The system is explicitly designed to prefer a visible degraded state over silently discarding work.
Main reliability risks
Mutation completion and persistence completion are not consistently the same event
Homework is the clearest example. A mutation may appear successful and emit update events before IndexedDB durability is known.
A single canonical contract should distinguish:
State accepted in memory.

Save scheduled.

Save committed.

Save verified.

Save failed and recovered.

Structured data and attachment bytes span separate databases
That is a reasonable design, but operations crossing those databases cannot be one native IndexedDB transaction. Sutra compensates with attachment links, completeness checks, cleanup, and recovery. This remains an area where crashes can create orphans or temporarily incomplete records.
Live bindings can diverge from appData
The application has guards around import and hydration because serializing stale editor or runtime values back into appData can overwrite newer canonical values. That is evidence of the architectural risk, even though several known cases are handled.
Some optional-feature failures can still propagate
The asynchronous feature guard problem means a rejected optional initialization can both mark the feature degraded and remain observable as an unhandled rejection.
Coordination lacks an explicit timeout model
Web Locks and local queues are used thoughtfully, but a hung callback can indefinitely hold a logical operation unless the browser or page lifecycle breaks it.
Reliability verdict
For ordinary student data, Sutra is more careful than most local applications. Reliability is held back by inconsistent completion semantics and the difficulty of proving behavior across the central runtime.
Testing Assessment
What the test suite gives real confidence in
The strongest confidence exists around:
Sync protocol logic.

Cryptography integration.

Merge and conflict behavior.

Data isolation.

Backup and restore.

Locked-note confidentiality.

Core migrations.

Import normalization.

Responsive navigation.

Modal lifecycle.

Recovery behavior.

Hostile DOM handling.

Exact deployment artifact integrity.

These tests target properties and failure modes, not only happy-path screenshots.
Where quantity overstates quality
Several tests assert source strings, selector presence, or expected file placement. These are useful architectural guardrails, especially in a no-build codebase, but they do not prove the runtime behavior is correct.
The accessibility suite is the clearest weak point. Some conditions cannot fail, some violations are warnings, and only a subset of controls is sampled.
Important missing or insufficiently enforced tests
The next highest-value tests would cover:
Private documents explicitly supplied to assistant context.

Homework mutation rollback when canonical IndexedDB persistence fails.

Actual production response headers.

Optional-feature promise rejection behavior.

No continued polling after a feature is hidden or unmounted.

Performance budgets for initial script parse and cache installation.

Complete accessible-name and target-size enforcement.

Feature-pack load failure followed by retry.

Navigation state without observer or timer-based reconciliation.

Vendored dependency inventory freshness.

Testing verdict
The suite is a major asset, but “many tests” should not become a reason to defer architectural cleanup. Tests are currently acting as a safety cage around complexity that should also be reduced.
Performance Assessment
No benchmark run was performed, so this section identifies architectural bottlenecks rather than claiming measured regressions.
1. JavaScript parse and execution
The 4.85 MB core runtime and long eager script chain create unavoidable parsing and execution cost. Even cached scripts must be parsed and initialized.
2. Optional capabilities are often loaded before they are used
The Editor v2 vendor bundle is loaded even though the editor is opt-in. Slides, Sheets, Canvas, PDF infrastructure, customization, and academic modules also load into the base application path.
3. Service-worker installation is oversized
The critical cache contains a very large PDF resource set. A failure anywhere in a critical addAll group can make installation fail as a whole.
A better model would distinguish:
Minimal offline shell.

Core daily-workflow assets.

Feature-on-demand caches.

Large optional PDF language resources.

User-triggered offline downloads.

4. Whole-workspace operations scale with user data
Serializing, cloning, hashing, projecting, and normalizing the complete workspace becomes more expensive as the student accumulates notes, tasks, histories, settings, and feature data.
5. Polling substitutes for lifecycle events
Slides and Sheets periodically inspect the current page even though route and page-load events already exist. Polling costs are small individually but accumulate as more feature scripts follow the pattern.
6. Sheets scroll work is unnecessarily broad
Virtualizing cell DOM is correct, but rebuilding 10,000-row offsets and reevaluating the workbook during every scroll can become the dominant cost for complex workbooks.
7. CSS matching and precedence are broad
Large global stylesheets and extensive selectors increase style recalculation cost and make it more difficult to reason about which changes cause layout work.
Performance verdict
Performance is unlikely to be solved through micro-optimizing individual loops alone. The major gains will come from reducing the amount of code and data involved in each lifecycle event.
Security & Privacy Assessment
Boundary
	Assessment
	
Local workspace
	Strong local-first default. Structured data is not encrypted at rest merely because it is local.
	
Portable backup
	Strong encrypted .sutra path; sensitive fields and private-document content are intentionally redacted from plain JSON.
	
Sutra Sync
	Strong E2EE design and server authorization; metadata remains visible to the service.
	
Provider credentials
	Session-only default is good. Remembered vault resists casual storage extraction but not same-origin malicious code.
	
Workspace lock
	Correctly presented as a privacy screen, not encryption.
	
Locked notes
	Strong shared authorization boundary and cross-surface tests.
	
Assistant context
	Bounded and permission-filtered; private-document policy has a latent omission bug.
	
Assistant actions
	Review-before-apply and source-validation contracts are strong.
	
Plugins
	Strong sandbox and capability model.
	
DOM/XSS
	Good sanitizer and guardrails, but broad CSP and numerous inherited HTML sinks raise impact.
	
Deployment headers
	Intended policy is stronger than the policy proven on the actual GitHub Pages deployment.
	
Sync revocation
	Thoughtful verified wipe flow; offline devices necessarily cannot receive revocation until they reconnect.
	
Key security strengths
No required telemetry.

No required cloud account.

Strong sync cryptography.

Explicit local versus transmitted data receipts.

Secret-pattern redaction.

Locked-source handling.

Provider selection.

Session-only credential default.

Sandboxed plugins.

Input limits.

Safe URL schemes.

Local-only share/import processing.

RLS and account/device binding.

Key security weaknesses
CSP is not a strong containment boundary
unsafe-inline and broad provider origins mean CSP offers limited protection against a successful injection.
Same-origin compromise has high impact
Because Sutra intentionally keeps sensitive data and optionally decryptable credentials locally, any script running with Sutra’s origin can potentially access a large amount of private information.
Public production test hooks increase exposed surface
window.__sutraPublicBetaTestHooks exposes snapshots, chat state helpers, lock helpers, and other internal operations in production. These do not automatically bypass the underlying authorization checks, but test-only convenience APIs should not expand the production interface unnecessarily.
Server abuse controls are not evident at repository level
The inspected Sync schema has operation bounds, ownership checks, and locking. A comprehensive per-user storage quota, rate-limiting system, or abuse-monitoring layer was not evident in the reviewed repository. This may exist outside the repository, so it should be treated as an unverified operational area rather than a confirmed absence.
Security verdict
Sutra’s privacy engineering is substantially above average. The central risk is not weak cryptography; it is the web-origin security boundary around a large, permissive, globally coupled frontend.
UI Audit
Strongest aspects
A deliberate visual language exists
Sutra has a clear premium student-workspace direction, with dark navy surfaces, restrained accent colors, soft elevation, serif display typography, and spacious document areas. The token and theme systems show deliberate authorship rather than default framework styling.
Core interaction states are standardized
Focus-visible, disabled, modal layering, reduced motion, touch targets, safe-area handling, empty states, and error states have central contracts.
Empty states generally provide action
The live product does not merely say “No data.” Many surfaces explain what belongs there and present the next action, such as adding a task, configuring a course, starting review, or opening settings. (Tanuj Ranjith)
Notes receives appropriate context
The Notes tree and editor controls are shown where they are relevant rather than consuming space across every product area.
Sync and backup UI is unusually transparent
Setup explains recovery limitations, passphrase responsibility, encrypted safety backups, conflicts, and offline revocation behavior. That builds trust more effectively than vague “secure cloud” language. (Tanuj Ranjith)
Weakest aspects
Component consistency is not guaranteed
Many dialogs, drawers, panels, alerts, pickers, toolbars, and empty states were implemented independently. Central contracts help, but the underlying markup and behavior remain heterogeneous.
Settings are very dense
Search and categories improve the experience, but Settings has become the home for feature packs, AI providers, credentials, context permissions, editor modes, themes, plugins, backups, Sync, Drive, onboarding controls, accessibility, and many product-specific switches.
Visual identity is diluted by theme breadth
Sutra, Dark, Botanical, Peach, glass effects, platform-inspired themes, and cinematic presets demonstrate customization capability. They also make the product’s canonical visual identity less clear and multiply the testing surface.
Some desktop-class tools look embedded rather than fully integrated
Slides and Sheets use their own dense toolbars, side inspectors, document tabs, dialogs, and keyboard models. They are capable, but their implementation and lifecycle still feel more like inserted mini-apps than mature Sutra-native surfaces.
Legacy precedence affects polish
When visual correctness depends on late files, inline !important, and repair modules, subtle inconsistencies in spacing, active states, and responsive behavior become more likely.
UX Audit
The core mental model is strong
The core Sutra loop is understandable:
Capture work.

See what is due.

Plan it on the Timeline.

Work from Notes.

Focus.

Review.

Back up or synchronize.

The Today page acts as a command center rather than a separate data silo. Homework, Timeline, Notes, and Review are connected enough to feel like parts of one system.
Progressive disclosure is directionally correct
Advanced feature packs are disabled by default for new users. More specialized surfaces are moved behind secondary navigation or Settings. The Assistant is optional rather than imposed.
Trust and recoverability are excellent UX
Sutra tells users when a save is degraded, distinguishes backup from sync, offers recovery mode, exposes emergency export, presents conflicts rather than silently resolving them, and requires review before destructive or AI-generated changes.
This is some of Sutra’s best UX work.
The product’s peripheral mental model is weaker
Several concepts overlap:
Homework versus Tasks versus All Due.

Timeline versus Calendar.

Review versus Testing Hub versus AP Study versus Cram Hub.

College versus College App.

Backup versus Drive Sync versus Sutra Sync.

Notes versus Canvas versus Slides versus Sheets versus HTML pages.

Life tracking inside an academic workspace.

Business tools inside a student operating system.

These distinctions may be valid, but each requires explanation and increases the chance that users do not know where an item belongs.
Terminology drift increases onboarding friction
Home, Today, Create, Notes, workspace, page, note, document, and view are not always used consistently. A canonical vocabulary should be applied in onboarding, navigation, commands, empty states, documentation, and code-facing labels.
Prototype controls remain visible
A visible “Reset onboarding status (testing)” control and several experimental labels make parts of the product feel less final than the core privacy and sync systems. (Tanuj Ranjith)
UX verdict
Sutra feels cohesive when used as a student planner and note system. It becomes less cohesive as users move into the outer rings of Life, Business, extensive customization, and office-suite-style editing.
Mobile / Responsive Audit
What works
The daily mobile shell is convincingly adapted:
Bottom navigation instead of compressed desktop tabs.

Secondary route sheet.

Safe-area insets.

Touch-target contracts.

Notes-specific drawer.

Focus trapping.

Browser-history integration.

Reduced-motion handling.

Responsive boundary tests around 640 and 641 pixels.

Pixel, iPhone, and iPad Playwright configurations.

These are substantial strengths.
What remains risky
Global gestures depend on exclusions
Document-level swipe and pull handlers must recognize every editor, range input, canvas, scrollable panel, selected text region, and future interactive surface. As Sutra adds features, the exclusion list becomes an ongoing maintenance obligation.
Advanced editors remain desktop-oriented
Slides, Sheets, PDF workspaces, large inspectors, spreadsheet grids, and document toolbars are inherently constrained on phones. Responsive CSS can make them fit, but that does not automatically make them efficient mobile workflows.
Late mobile CSS remains load-bearing
Mobile correctness is still partly produced by a large late override sheet rather than component-owned responsive behavior.
Mobile verdict
The mobile experience for Today, Homework, Notes, Timeline, and navigation is one of Sutra’s stronger UX areas. The office-suite surfaces remain closer to “available on mobile” than “designed for mobile.”
Consistency Audit
Interaction consistency
Good: Shared confirmation dialogs, modal manager, focus contracts, toasts, review-before-apply actions.
Inconsistent: Browser prompts in Sheets, bespoke alert fallbacks, different overlay implementations, independent toolbar models, and mixed polling/event-driven lifecycle behavior.
State consistency
Good: One canonical persisted workspace and an emerging entity registry.
Inconsistent: Live globals, mirrored editor DOM, feature-local arrays, bridge properties, DOM-derived route state, and fire-and-forget persistence calls.
Navigation consistency
Good: Canonical route metadata and a responsive mobile projection.
Inconsistent: Home versus Today, Create versus Notes, direct tabs versus overflow groups, and modules that repair visibility after other modules render.
Visual consistency
Good: Tokens, focus style, z-index ladder, semantic colors, surface variables.
Inconsistent: Large legacy cascade, duplicate token families, inline styles, !important, bespoke component CSS, and extensive theme overrides.
Naming consistency
The remaining Atelier, Flow, NoteFlow, cw, hw, Sutra, page, note, workspace, and document terminology makes it harder to determine which names are canonical and which are compatibility residue.
Privacy consistency
Privacy intent is generally strong and centralized. The latent privateDocuments assistant-filter defect shows why privacy claims should be enforced at the final outbound boundary rather than inferred from what current context builders happen not to include.

Highest-Leverage Improvements
1. Make the assistant privacy boundary structurally deny-by-default
Problem: privateDocuments is not actually removed if supplied to the policy helper.
Recommended direction: Treat all context fields as denied unless explicitly mapped and approved. Apply the same filter again immediately before constructing the provider request. Add a test supplying private-document metadata and bytes.
Expected impact: Removes a latent high-sensitivity regression class.
Scope: Small.
2. Align real production hosting with the intended header policy
Problem: The strong policy lives in Vercel configuration while production is published through GitHub Pages.
Recommended direction: Use a deployment surface that can enforce the intended headers, or explicitly redesign the policy around what the actual host supports. Add live response-header verification to deployment.
Expected impact: Strengthens the browser security boundary around local data and remembered credentials.
Scope: Medium.
3. Replace unsafe-inline incrementally
Problem: The current CSP cannot strongly contain script injection.
Recommended direction: Move remaining inline executable code and event handlers into external scripts, then transition to hashes, nonces, or a strict external-script policy. Keep the current sink ratchet, but add an explicit CSP migration budget.
Expected impact: Reduces the impact of accidental HTML injection and compromised content paths.
Scope: Large.
4. Create one persistence completion contract
Problem: Different features interpret “save” as in-memory mutation, scheduled save, or committed IndexedDB transaction.
Recommended direction: Introduce one receipt or promise contract for canonical mutations. It should distinguish scheduled, committed, verified, conflicted, and failed states. Route Homework and Assistant-created Homework changes through it.
Expected impact: Eliminates misleading save success and enables reliable rollback.
Scope: Medium.
5. Continue decomposing app.js through ownership transfer
Problem: The central runtime owns too much.
Recommended direction: Do not split it arbitrarily by line range. Extract one complete ownership boundary at a time:
Persistence orchestration.

Page and space store.

Route state.

Modal and overlay service.

Editor lifecycle.

Import/export orchestration.

Settings and preference store.

Each extraction should remove the old global responsibility rather than create another mirror.
Expected impact: Largest long-term improvement to development speed and regression risk.
Scope: Architectural.
6. Establish one route and shell state owner
Problem: Navigation modules repair each other through DOM observation and delayed retries.
Recommended direction: Route state should be data, not inferred from DOM classes. Desktop tabs, mobile dock, More sheet, contextual sidebars, and custom tabs should render from the same route snapshot.
Expected impact: Removes timing-sensitive UI fixes and simplifies navigation testing.
Scope: Large.
7. Move advanced feature code to demand-driven loading
Problem: Many optional editors and modules load during base startup.
Recommended direction: Keep the daily loop in the base shell. Load Editor v2 only when enabled, PDF assets when a PDF opens, Slides/Sheets when those page types open, and optional packs when activated.
Expected impact: Faster startup, less memory, and smaller parse cost.
Scope: Large.
8. Split service-worker assets into cache tiers
Problem: Full PDF resources are treated as critical installation assets.
Recommended direction: Use a small atomic shell cache, a core-workflow cache, and feature caches populated on demand. Large CMaps and specialized font resources should not determine whether the base PWA installs.
Expected impact: More reliable installation and updates, especially on mobile networks.
Scope: Medium to Large.
9. Remove feature polling in favor of lifecycle events
Problem: Slides and Sheets continually inspect page state.
Recommended direction: Mount, activate, suspend, and dispose feature surfaces in response to explicit page and route lifecycle events. Timers should have owners and teardown.
Expected impact: Less background work and clearer feature state.
Scope: Medium.
10. Enforce accessibility rather than recording it
Problem: Some accessibility tests log defects or contain vacuous assertions.
Recommended direction: Add an automated accessibility engine, fail on serious violations, test every primary view, and keep targeted keyboard tests for custom editors and navigation.
Expected impact: Converts accessibility intent into dependable product quality.
Scope: Medium.
11. Reduce legacy CSS by component ownership
Problem: Link order and !important are behavioral dependencies.
Recommended direction: Choose high-change components first, such as navigation, dialogs, editor shell, Settings, and Today cards. Give each one a documented DOM and token contract, migrate its rules, then delete the corresponding legacy selectors.
Expected impact: Fewer visual regressions and easier UI evolution.
Scope: Large.
12. Add repository release protections
Problem: Direct pushes to unprotected main deploy production.
Recommended direction: Require CI and deploy-artifact verification before merge, protect main, use pull requests for production changes, and consider signed release commits.
Expected impact: Prevents accidental release bypass.
Scope: Small.
13. Introduce performance budgets
Problem: There is no clear limit on base script, stylesheet, precache, or startup growth.
Recommended direction: Track base transfer size, uncompressed parse size, critical cache size, startup time, long tasks, and representative workspace save duration.
Expected impact: Prevents performance from deteriorating invisibly as features are added.
Scope: Medium.
14. Create a vendored-dependency inventory
Problem: Major runtimes sit outside normal package auditing.
Recommended direction: Record package, version, source, license, checksum, build modifications, last review date, and relevant advisories for every vendored runtime.
Expected impact: Improves security maintenance and upgrade confidence.
Scope: Small to Medium.
15. Consolidate the product vocabulary
Problem: Home, Today, Create, Notes, page, note, and document overlap.
Recommended direction: Define one user-facing information architecture and apply it across onboarding, navigation, Settings, empty states, commands, documentation, and feature packs.
Expected impact: Meaningful improvement to first-time comprehension at relatively low engineering cost.
Scope: Medium.
Things I Would NOT Change
1. Do not abandon local-first authority
This is central to Sutra’s identity and privacy model.
2. Do not immediately normalize the entire workspace into dozens of IndexedDB stores
The portable root object supports backup, import, and deterministic sync. Improve mutation boundaries first. Normalize only where scale or atomicity clearly requires it.
3. Do not rewrite Sutra wholesale in React, Vue, or another framework
A framework migration would combine architectural change, UI change, persistence risk, and product regression into one project. Introduce enforceable module boundaries incrementally.
4. Do not replace the Sync protocol merely because the frontend architecture is strained
Sync is not the source of the central maintainability problem.
5. Do not remove the classic editor fallback prematurely
The Editor v2 compatibility bridge is careful, but the fallback still protects existing documents and unsupported edge cases.
6. Do not weaken review-before-apply behavior
Assistant actions, imports, schedules, cleanup, and destructive operations should remain previewable and recoverable.
7. Do not remove Safe Mode or emergency export
These are among Sutra’s most production-minded capabilities.
8. Do not discard vendoring merely to reduce repository size
Vendoring supports offline reliability. Improve inventory and demand-driven loading instead.
9. Do not remove contextual mobile navigation
The mobile dock, More sheet, and Notes-specific drawer are good product decisions.
10. Do not optimize away privacy transparency
Sync warnings, passphrase responsibility, provider disclosures, response receipts, and workspace-lock limitations should remain explicit.
Final Verdict
How healthy is the codebase?
Sutra is operationally healthier than it is structurally healthy.
Its data-safety systems, tests, migrations, recovery, synchronization, and release pipeline make it surprisingly resilient. Its global runtime, CSS architecture, persistence bridge inconsistencies, and feature lifecycle make it difficult to maintain.
Is the architecture still appropriate for Sutra’s current size?
The static local-first architecture is appropriate.
The internal global-monolith architecture is no longer appropriate for Sutra’s current feature count. It has reached the point where adding another major surface without first reducing ownership ambiguity will make the product harder to stabilize.
What will become painful as Sutra grows?
The first pain points will be:
Safely changing app.js.

Understanding route and UI ownership.

Keeping mobile overrides consistent.

Preserving save semantics across every feature.

Avoiding slow startup.

Testing every theme and editor combination.

Updating vendored libraries.

Preventing peripheral features from diluting the core product.

Onboarding another experienced engineer.

Does the product feel cohesive?
The daily student loop feels cohesive.
The complete feature catalog feels partially cohesive. Notes, Homework, Today, Timeline, Focus, Review, and Testing belong together. College planning is adjacent and understandable. Some Life, Business, theme, plugin, and office-suite capabilities feel more like extensions sharing Sutra’s shell than one unified student workflow.
Which parts feel production-grade?
Sutra Sync.

Encrypted backups.

Recovery and Safe Mode.

Locked-note authorization.

Import review.

Storage hygiene.

Exact-artifact deployment.

Core responsive navigation.

Privacy disclosures.

Several migration and normalization systems.

Which parts still feel prototype-grade?
The 4.85 MB global kernel.

UI repair modules.

Slides and Sheets lifecycle.

Duplicate feature implementations.

Polling-based activation.

Some Settings and onboarding vocabulary.

Accessibility enforcement.

Browser prompts in advanced editors.

Production test hooks.

Unprotected release governance.

What are the largest risks?
A cross-feature regression caused by changing the central runtime.

A script injection gaining access to local workspace data or remembered credentials.

A feature reporting success before persistence is durable.

Startup and cache cost growing until mobile use becomes unreliable.

Product breadth outpacing information-architecture consolidation.

Tests preserving complicated implementation structure rather than enabling its simplification.

What would concern an experienced engineer inheriting Sutra?
The engineer would be most concerned by:
The size and responsibility of app.js.

Global mutable contracts.

Load-order coupling.

CSS precedence.

DOM-observed state.

Fire-and-forget persistence adapters.

Numerous compatibility and repair layers.

The effort required to determine which implementation is canonical.

Direct production deployment from unprotected main.

What would impress that engineer?
The engineer would be impressed by:
The seriousness of Sync.

The attention to data recovery.

Cross-surface locked-note tests.

The breadth of failure-mode coverage.

The exact-artifact release pipeline.

Transparent privacy UX.

Review-first imports and Assistant actions.

The amount of defensive normalization.

The fact that a static browser application has sophisticated conflict, recovery, and migration behavior.

GOOD: Data protection, encrypted Sync, recovery, backup, release discipline, locked-note privacy, mobile navigation, and several newer domain abstractions.
MID: Product breadth, state-root strategy, modular extraction, CSS migration, accessibility enforcement, feature loading, newer document editors, and credential-vault positioning.
BAD: The 4.85 MB global runtime, fragmented UI ownership, permissive and deployment-misaligned security headers, non-durable mutation semantics, eager loading, polling, and unprotected production governance.
Biggest strength: Sutra treats student data loss and privacy failure as first-class engineering problems.
Biggest weakness: Too much product behavior still depends on one global runtime and its surrounding compatibility layers.
Most important next investment: Incrementally extract authoritative state, route, and persistence ownership from app.js, while first closing the assistant privacy, production-header, and durable-save gaps.
Sutra Full Audit
Executive Summary
Sutra is a technically uneven but substantially hardened product. Its persistence, encrypted backups, multi-device sync, failure recovery, deployment pipeline, privacy boundaries, and principal student-facing screens are much stronger than its underlying application architecture.
The most accurate description is a carefully guarded monolith:
The safety-critical perimeter is often production-grade.

The central runtime and CSS architecture still reflect prototype-era growth.

The default student workflow is increasingly coherent.

The full product has accumulated more scope than its information architecture and loading model can comfortably support.

The largest current risk is not an obvious catastrophic bug. It is change amplification, where one feature can require coordinated edits across the global runtime, static shell, CSS ordering, cache stamps, service worker manifests, compatibility aliases, persistence inventory, tests, and documentation.

Measured directly from the supplied ZIP:
src/core/app.js is approximately 4.85 MB and 85,393 lines.

styles/base/styles.css is approximately 1.01 MB and 35,316 lines.

Sutra.html is approximately 649 KB and 8,916 lines.

The shell references 105 external or local scripts totaling approximately 8.25 MB of uncompressed JavaScript, plus 44 stylesheets totaling approximately 2.09 MB, before considering HTML and other assets.

The static shell contains roughly 6,345 DOM elements before feature-specific runtime rendering.

The styles directory contains approximately 69,000 lines of CSS and roughly 2,871 uses of !important.

The repository contains more than 500 unit-side cases and more than 500 browser-side cases when parameterized tests are included.

Those numbers do not automatically make the application bad, but they accurately explain why changes have become expensive and why extensive guardrails are now necessary.
Approximate ratings
Area
	Rating
	Assessment
	
Engineering / Codebase
	6.3/10
	Strong subsystem engineering, weakened by an oversized central runtime and implicit dependencies.
	
Architecture
	4.7/10
	The architecture still functions, but global scope, load-order coupling, and monolithic state ownership have exceeded a comfortable scale.
	
Reliability
	7.7/10
	Persistence, recovery, migrations, backups, and sync are unusually defensive. Reliability is constrained by the number of mutation paths feeding them.
	
Maintainability
	4.0/10
	This is the weakest engineering dimension. Changes require too much repository-wide knowledge and coordination.
	
UI
	8.2/10
	The core visual identity is polished, distinctive, and generally coherent. Secondary controls and advanced surfaces are less disciplined.
	
UX
	6.8/10
	The daily student loop is strong; the complete feature set creates competing mental models and discoverability costs.
	
Performance
	4.6/10
	The eager payload, large DOM, giant CSS cascade, and whole-workspace operations impose an increasingly expensive baseline.
	
Testing
	7.1/10
	Excellent breadth and release coverage, but test signal varies sharply. Some suites prove behavior; others mostly prove that code or DOM still exists.
	
Security / Privacy Engineering
	7.6/10
	Encryption, sanitization, permissions, plugin isolation, and fail-closed behavior are strong. Remote parser loading, plaintext safety snapshots, and CSP debt reduce the score.
	
Overall Product Coherence
	6.7/10
	The student command-center concept is coherent. College, life, business, document, cloud, AI, and customization capabilities do not yet feel fully consolidated around it.
	
These scores are directional judgments, not measurements. The unusual aspect of Sutra is the gap between categories: its data-safety engineering is materially better than its maintainability, and its visual polish is materially better than its frontend composition.
Audit Basis and Limitations
The audit used both GitHub main and the supplied ZIP. The checked root files and src/core/app.js matched between the two sources, so the ZIP was a credible snapshot of the repository revision inspected.
The assessment included:
repository-wide structural and size analysis

major runtime and persistence flows

migrations, encrypted backups, sync, credentials, plugins, Assistant permissions, service worker, deployment configuration, and guardrails

unit and Playwright test source

the current public Sutra interface

the existing desktop and mobile screenshots included in the repository

The repository remained unchanged. I did not execute the complete verification suite because the documented commands create output such as .tmp, .deploy, Playwright traces, browser profiles, reports, and potentially downloaded dependencies, which would violate the strict read-only requirement. Therefore:
I am evaluating test design and coverage, not claiming that every test currently passes.

Performance conclusions are based on payload, DOM, CSS, state-flow, and benchmark structure, not a new production performance trace.

Authenticated Supabase, Drive, provider-backup, and cross-device operations were reviewed from code and tests, not exercised against live user accounts.

UI conclusions are strongest for the principal screens represented by the live shell and supplied screenshots.

What Is GOOD
1. Workspace persistence and data-loss prevention
Classification: GOOD
This is Sutra’s strongest engineering area.
The persistence layer does much more than write a JSON object to IndexedDB. It includes:
reusable IndexedDB connection management

blocked-upgrade and versionchange handling

atomic conditional writes

stale-write protection

previous meaningful root recovery

confirmed-root markers

startup write blocking after an uncertain or failed read

serialized write coordination

cross-tab coordination through Web Locks and BroadcastChannel

read-back verification

explicit storage-health reporting

emergency export paths

separate treatment of canonical workspace failures and secondary localStorage failures

workspace-db.js performs conditional compare-and-write operations inside a single transaction, retaining recovery information and commit markers alongside the canonical root. The coordinator adds cross-tab exclusivity where supported while retaining a local queue fallback.
The data documentation also makes meaningful distinctions between the canonical workspace, attachment bytes, Homework’s compatibility mirror, local preferences, credentials, and recovery journals. That distinction matters because it prevents a Homework storage error from being misreported as total workspace loss.
Why this is good: Local-first applications fail differently from server-backed applications. Sutra does not assume a successful API request means durability. It actively verifies local persistence and gives the user actionable recovery options.
Preserve: The atomic root transaction, confirmed-root marker, startup write block, read-back verification, and separation of workspace health from secondary-store health should survive any architectural modernization.
2. Sutra Sync’s deterministic and encrypted design
Classification: GOOD
The incremental Sync subsystem is considerably cleaner than the application core around it.
Its most important properties are:
a pure protocol layer

deterministic operation ordering

field-aware three-way merging

semantic comparison for selected data types

top-level rich-text block merging

dedicated conflict records instead of silently materializing conflict pages

stable conflict identity

explicit tombstone handling

offline outbox behavior

authenticated routing metadata

encrypted operations, snapshots, and attachment bytes

account-scoped operational state

fail-closed behavior on account or device-session mismatch

The encryption layer uses AES-GCM with fresh IVs and binds routing metadata as authenticated additional data. The wrapped vault key uses PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 with 600,000 iterations.
The merge engine’s determinism contract is unusually explicit. It does not rely on wall-clock time to resolve concurrent changes, and it retains both incompatible values for review rather than silently discarding one.
The corresponding tests are behavioral rather than superficial. They exercise independent edits, same-record field merges, rich-text block conflicts, delete-versus-edit behavior, ordering, convergence from both directions, and deterministic conflict identity.
The browser suite also uses isolated contexts to represent separate devices and a shared mocked server, covering opt-in behavior, account switching, vault failures, identity creation, convergence, and remote state.
Why this is good: Sutra Sync is designed as a replication protocol, not as an afterthought attached to save events.
Preserve: Deterministic merge, conflict review, authenticated metadata, ciphertext-only server assumptions, local-save independence, and account-scoped operational state.
3. Encrypted backups and portability discipline
Classification: GOOD
The .sutra format is designed around an authenticated encrypted envelope rather than an ordinary ZIP with a misleading file extension.
The implementation and documentation specify:
AES-GCM-256

a fresh salt and IV per manual export

PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA-256 with 600,000 iterations

authenticated envelope headers

checksummed internal assets

extracted binary attachment packaging

explicit secret stripping

legacy .sutra and .atelier compatibility

failure when required attachment bytes are missing

import validation before workspace mutation

versioned migrations

preservation of unknown fields and quarantined recovery data

The portability inventory classifies top-level fields, nested durable contracts, device-local data, secrets, reconstructed values, assets, and compatibility fields. This is one of the more disciplined parts of the repository.
The migration registry also validates serializability and relationships, preserves unknown fields, and quarantines malformed collection shapes instead of silently dropping them.
Why this is good: Portability is treated as an explicit schema contract, not as “serialize whatever happens to be in memory.”
Preserve: The encrypted envelope, attachment completeness refusal, checksums, unknown-field preservation, recovery quarantine, and compatibility imports.
4. Exact-artifact release engineering
Classification: GOOD
The deployment workflow builds the production artifact once, tests that exact artifact, uploads the already-tested output, deploys without rebuilding, and then performs a live smoke check.
The pull-request workflow similarly separates static and unit validation from browser testing while passing the verified deploy artifact between jobs. The scheduled compatibility matrix runs Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, and responsive projects against the packaged output.
The Playwright configuration includes desktop Chrome, Chromium, Firefox, WebKit, Pixel, iPhone, iPad, and narrow-desktop projects.
Why this is good: It closes the common gap where CI validates one set of files while deployment rebuilds or packages another.
Preserve: Build once, test the artifact, deploy without rebuilding, then smoke-test the deployment.
5. Central safety and observability services
Classification: GOOD
Sutra has built shared infrastructure for recurring cross-cutting risks:
dom-safety.js for user HTML sanitization, trusted templates, URL checks, style filtering, and sandboxed rendering

error-reporter.js for a local bounded diagnostics ring, secret scrubbing, global error capture, and optional user-facing messages

feature guards that isolate feature initialization failures

startup-health checks for catastrophic boot failures

storage wrappers for noncanonical local storage

static guardrails for raw sinks, direct storage calls, and unregistered globals

The DOM sanitizer defaults to escaping when it cannot safely parse, removes dangerous subtrees, validates URL schemes, filters inline CSS, and distinguishes user content from developer-authored templates.
The error reporter scrubs common credential forms from messages, stacks, contexts, and URLs before placing them into exportable diagnostics. It also deduplicates bursts and remains local-only.
Why this is good: These mechanisms turn several historically scattered concerns into auditable boundaries.
Preserve: The centralized APIs and their fail-safe behavior. The next step should be reducing the legacy exceptions they currently surround.
6. Mobile navigation delegates to canonical navigation
Classification: GOOD
The mobile shell does not maintain an independent route registry. It discovers enabled canonical .view-tab elements and delegates navigation through their existing click handlers. This avoids a common mobile regression where desktop and mobile navigation drift into separate products.
The mobile implementation also includes:
a prioritized student-loop bottom bar

an accessible “All sections” sheet

focus trapping and restoration

browser Back integration

Notes page-drawer handling

unread notification mirroring

gesture exclusions around editors and interactive regions

reduced-motion-aware haptics

canonical Capture action delegation

The supplied mobile Today screenshot also shows a convincing adaptation rather than a compressed desktop page. The hierarchy remains clear, the bottom navigation is usable, and save status remains visible.
Preserve: Canonical route delegation and the student-loop priority order.
7. Distinctive visual identity on principal screens
Classification: GOOD
The strongest screens, particularly Today, Notes, Homework, Timeline, Testing Hub, and Assistant, share a recognizable visual language:
warm neutral surfaces

restrained gold accenting

editorial serif headings paired with functional sans-serif controls

generous primary-content spacing

high-quality card composition

consistent rounded geometry

a calmer tone than typical productivity dashboards

The Notes editor is especially successful. It creates a clear writing-focused canvas while retaining page navigation and contextual tools. Today also succeeds at presenting a “what matters now” hierarchy rather than starting with analytics.
The live shell confirms that these are real product surfaces rather than isolated mockups. (tanujranjith.github.io)
Preserve: Typography, surface treatment, restrained color system, writing-canvas emphasis, and Today’s priority-first hierarchy.
8. Plugin isolation and Assistant permission boundaries
Classification: GOOD
Local plugins are not allowed to execute directly in the host page. Runtime plugins are placed inside an iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" but without allow-same-origin, a restrictive CSP, no network access, no host storage access, and an explicit postMessage operation allowlist. Imported runtime-capable plugins return disabled and require review.
Assistant context is filtered through explicit permissions for notes, planning, learning, College, courses, life, business, and memory. Locked-note contents, wellness, financial data, and private documents receive additional gates. Consequential actions require approval-derived permissions.
Why this is good: Extensibility and AI are treated as permissioned capabilities rather than trusted internal code.
Preserve: Sandboxed plugin execution, imported-code re-review, bounded bridge operations, per-area Assistant permissions, and approval before consequential actions.
9. Service-worker update and caching policy
Classification: GOOD
The service worker:
intercepts only same-origin GET requests

excludes cross-origin AI and provider traffic

uses network-first behavior for navigations

uses exact versioned URLs for cache-first static assets

refuses to install with a partial critical cache

does not activate underneath an open workspace without user consent

restricts share-target content by type, file count, file size, total size, and lifetime

Preserve: Network-first documents, exact versioned asset caching, safe update activation, and exclusion of user/provider traffic.
10. Technical debt is documented rather than denied
Classification: GOOD
The repository’s architecture documentation accurately identifies that:
classic scripts share a global namespace

folders are organizational rather than actual module boundaries

CSS link order is load-bearing

app.js decomposition must proceed through safe seams

some functions cannot be extracted because of closure dependencies

legacy CSS should shrink rather than grow

moving files affects checks, manifests, shell links, documentation, and cache controls

This documentation does not remove the debt, but it materially reduces the probability of careless damage.
What Is MID
1. The static, no-build model
Classification: MID
A static browser application is well aligned with several Sutra goals:
no mandatory server

optional accounts

easy static hosting

offline support

direct local operation

low deployment complexity

fewer mandatory third-party dependencies

The problem is not static deployment. The problem is equating static deployment with classic scripts, a shared global scope, manual load order, and no build-time module graph.
The source documentation explicitly states that all scripts share a global namespace and that directories do not create module boundaries.
At the original scale, this was acceptable. At an 85,000-line core runtime with more than 100 scripts, it creates too much implicit coupling.
Recommended judgment: Preserve static deployability, but introduce build-time structure, modules, generated manifests, and enforceable dependency boundaries. A build step does not require turning Sutra into a server-backed SaaS.
2. Progressive disclosure without equivalent runtime separation
Classification: MID
Sutra correctly hides advanced areas by default. The student defaults emphasize Today, Homework, Notes, Timeline, and Review, while College, Life, Business, Assistant, and broader academic systems are opt-in.
That is good product disclosure. It is only partial technical disclosure.
