The declarative feature manifest currently contains true lazy definitions for Business and Assistant, while most other major areas remain represented in the eagerly loaded shell and script graph.
Consequence: Users see fewer features, but their browsers still pay much of the parsing, CSS, DOM, and memory cost.
Direction: Extend the manifest model to the remaining advanced surfaces and mount views only when they are visited.
3. Test breadth versus test signal
Classification: MID
The suite is large, broad, and integrated into release engineering. That is valuable.
However, a notable portion of the “unit” layer reads source files, extracts functions, evaluates snippets in VM contexts, or asserts that particular source strings and patterns remain present. These tests help protect compatibility and architecture conventions, but they are not equivalent to executable module-level behavior tests.
The contrast is visible inside the repository:
Sync merge tests directly execute pure modules and verify convergence.

Some chaos tests merely verify that document.body still contains children or even assert a literal true after an operation.

Consequence: The suite offers strong regression resistance in selected critical areas, but its raw case count overstates confidence in some general UI and failure scenarios.
Direction: Treat source-shape checks as architecture checks, not unit tests, and progressively replace weak behavioral simulations with executable public-API and user-flow tests.
4. Onboarding
Classification: MID
Onboarding demonstrates thoughtful product work:
it is consolidated instead of being spread across several old flows

it introduces the daily loop

it supports keyboard interaction and dismissal

it explains optional feature packs and protection

it lets students configure classes and initial setup

The weakness is conceptual load. A new student is being introduced to a large system before experiencing the simplest useful loop.
There is also terminology drift:
onboarding and product documentation increasingly use Home and Create

visible navigation and several implementation paths still use Today and Notes

This is small at the code level but meaningful in a first-run experience.
Direction: Let the first session establish Capture, Homework, Notes/Create, and Today/Home. Defer packs, cloud, advanced customization, and deeper configuration until after the first successful daily loop.
5. Settings and customization
Classification: MID
Settings is powerful and visually considered. Search, category navigation, previews, themes, density, plugins, integrations, privacy, data health, and feature controls are all valuable.
The weakness is that Settings has become an administrative application inside the application. It exposes a large amount of product and implementation complexity to the user.
Consequence: Advanced users gain control, but ordinary users can struggle to distinguish:
preferences from feature enablement

visual themes from layout modes

device-local settings from synced settings

Backup from Cloud Backup

Google Drive snapshot sync from Sutra Sync

privacy lock from encryption

Assistant permission modes from provider setup

Direction: Preserve depth, but introduce a simple default layer and an explicitly advanced layer.
6. Multiple cloud concepts
Classification: MID
The underlying distinctions are legitimate:
manual encrypted .sutra backup

provider-based cloud backup

Google Drive whole-snapshot sync

incremental Sutra Sync

local workspace saving

The documentation is technically clear about these differences.
The user-facing mental model remains difficult. A student should not have to understand replication architecture to know whether work is safe.
Direction: Present three user concepts:
Saved on this device

Backed up

Available on other devices

Provider and protocol details should sit behind those outcomes.
7. Error handling adoption
Classification: MID
The central reporter is strong, and critical persistence paths generally surface failures appropriately.
Across the complete runtime, there are still many catches that intentionally do nothing, silently fall back, or treat a feature failure as noncritical without recording context. Some are valid best-effort behavior, especially around cosmetic enhancements and unsupported browser APIs. The scale makes it hard to distinguish deliberate suppression from accidental masking.
Consequence: A feature can fail in a way that leaves the shell usable but gives neither the user nor diagnostics enough information to explain why.
Direction: Classify catches as:
expected capability absence

ignored cosmetic failure

diagnostic-only failure

user-impacting recoverable failure

data-integrity failure

Require an explicit treatment for each class.
8. Mobile coverage
Classification: MID
The mobile shell and Today experience are good. The code includes a dedicated mobile audit that walks four viewport shapes, eleven top-level views, and multiple deep surfaces.
The audit script is not part of the ordinary default verification path and uses a 32-pixel general touch-target warning floor, while the product documentation expects 44-pixel primary controls.
Complex surfaces such as Sheets, dense settings panels, College trackers, large tables, Timeline Week, and multi-pane editing remain more desktop-oriented.
Direction: Keep the adaptive shell, then establish hard mobile acceptance criteria for every enabled feature rather than relying predominantly on late CSS overrides.
9. Workspace privacy lock
Classification: MID
The lock is well implemented as a casual privacy screen and is notably honest about its limitations. The UI explicitly says it is not encryption at rest.
That is the correct representation.
It should not be confused with a fully encrypted local workspace, because an attacker with origin-data access or same-origin script execution can still reach underlying data.
Direction: Keep the lock. Do not market it as stronger than it is.
10. Upcoming Radar visualization
Classification: MID
Upcoming Radar is visually distinctive and reinforces Sutra’s brand. It is less effective as an information display than its styling suggests.
Problems include:
no obvious quantitative scale

overlapping central cards

limited chronological comparability

hidden overflow represented as “more”

decorative arcs competing with the task labels

lower scan efficiency than a well-ranked list

Direction: Preserve it as a compact summary or secondary visualization. Use a ranked chronological list as the primary deadline-inspection tool.
What Is BAD
No finding met my threshold for Critical based on the static evidence reviewed. I did find several High severity architectural and privacy risks.
1. The 85,000-line global core runtime
Classification: BAD
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic
src/core/app.js is approximately 85,393 lines and 4.85 MB. It still owns or directly coordinates:
the primary appData object

hydration and normalization

persistence orchestration

serialization and import/export

Notes and editor behavior

Timeline

view controllers

cloud-provider controllers

encrypted backup bridges

Google Drive snapshot behavior

Sync integration

search

focus timer

starter-pack application

many modals

feature wiring

The repository documentation itself acknowledges that app.js remains the global core and that many apparently extractable functions depend on helpers hidden inside its closures.
Impact:
Local reasoning becomes unreliable.

Small changes require broad regression testing.

Ownership is unclear.

Private closure dependencies prevent clean extraction.

Test isolation becomes difficult.

The global namespace becomes part of the dependency system.

New contributors must understand an excessive amount of context before safely editing one feature.

This is the biggest engineering weakness in Sutra.
2. Mutation and persistence are too widely coupled
Classification: BAD
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic
The persistence pipeline is robust, but too many places can mutate the state feeding it.
Measured from the current core, there are hundreds of persistence-triggering call sites and extensive synchronization between appData, feature globals, localStorage mirrors, editor state, attachment metadata, and UI state.
Homework is the clearest documented example: its live source remains localStorage while a copy is mirrored into the canonical workspace for portability.
The portability inventory also shows how broad the state graph has become, with dozens of top-level domains and many special nested contracts.
Impact:
A mutation may not be durable unless the correct persistence seam is triggered.

A stale editor or mirror can overwrite newer canonical state.

Import, sync, and cross-tab operations need numerous guards against ordinary runtime state.

New durable fields require coordinated changes across serialization, migration, normalization, Sync, import, export, and tests.

Recent fixes for stale writes, accidentally emptied workspaces, onboarding persistence, and false save conflicts indicate sustained regression pressure in this area.

The problem is not the persistence engine. The problem is the number of uncontrolled roads leading into it.
3. Excessive eager loading and static DOM
Classification: BAD
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic
The shell references approximately:
105 external or local scripts

8.25 MB of uncompressed JavaScript

44 stylesheets

2.09 MB of linked CSS

6,345 initial static elements

The browser may receive compressed responses, and repeat visits benefit from caching, but it still has to parse, compile, and manage the resulting runtime and cascade.
Only Business and Assistant are currently represented as truly optional lazy feature definitions.
Impact:
slower cold startup

larger main-thread parsing cost

higher memory use

longer style recalculation

hidden views remaining part of document complexity

poorer performance on school-issued and older mobile hardware

more costly global queries and listeners

more difficult performance diagnosis

Progressive disclosure in navigation is not enough. The implementation needs progressive loading and mounting.
4. CSS architecture has become structurally fragile
Classification: BAD
Severity: High
Scope: Systemic
The CSS layer has approximately:
69,000 lines

2,871 uses of !important

hundreds of media queries

overlapping breakpoint families

a 35,000-line base stylesheet

large theme overlays

multiple legacy override layers

late-loading mobile and hardening layers

The stylesheet documentation explicitly warns that link order is load-bearing and that legacy !important rules can override earlier layers.
Impact:
component styles are not locally predictable

responsive fixes can regress unrelated views

themes depend on override completeness

deleting an apparently redundant rule is risky

specificity escalates over time

visual bugs are fixed by adding another layer instead of resolving ownership

moving a stylesheet becomes an architectural operation

The documentation and checks prevent careless worsening, but the current cascade is still expensive to maintain.
5. Product scope has exceeded the current information architecture
Classification: BAD
Severity: High product risk
Scope: Systemic
Sutra now encompasses:
daily planning

Homework

Notes

Canvas

Slides

Sheets

HTML documents

PDF workspaces

Timeline

Review

AP Study

Testing Hub

Course Hub

grade forecasting

assignment planning

College applications

essay tracking

recommendations

scholarships

visits

life goals

habits

fitness

calories

sleep

wellness

journaling

spending

business projects

focus

custom dashboards

Assistant

plugins

themes

several cloud and backup models

The live application confirms that this breadth exists in the current product shell. (tanujranjith.github.io)
The issue is not that individual features are valueless. The issue is that too many features act as separate centers of gravity rather than feeding the same student loop.
Impact:
users must decide which subsystem owns a need

overlapping summaries compete for attention

settings become administrative

navigation terminology becomes inconsistent

every new feature expands persistence, Sync, backup, mobile, accessibility, and test obligations

product quality becomes harder to raise uniformly

Sutra should now consolidate rather than expand category coverage.
6. Automatic plaintext pre-import safety snapshots
Classification: BAD
Severity: High
Scope: Localized implementation with cross-cutting privacy and reliability impact
In the checked app.js:
src/core/app.js:63963–63980 builds and downloads a full JSON pre-import safety snapshot.

The filename explicitly includes UNENCRYPTED.

src/core/app.js:64207–64240 calls this safety-snapshot flow before full workspace replacement.

src/core/app.js:59298–59316 treats a synthetic browser anchor click as a successful download, although the application cannot verify that the browser actually persisted the file.

The snapshot strips credentials, but it can still contain plaintext notes, assignments, College information, wellness information, financial tracking, Assistant conversations, and other private workspace data.
This does not upload the data or prove external leakage. The risks are:
A user who otherwise uses encrypted .sutra files receives an automatic plaintext copy on disk.

The restore path may believe it has created a rollback file when a browser policy, download setting, sandbox, storage condition, or user action prevented persistence.

A cloud restore can create a local plaintext export as a side effect.

The safety mechanism and the privacy model work against one another.

Recommended direction: Use an atomic internal recovery root or journal as the primary rollback mechanism. Where an external safety file is needed, produce an encrypted .sutra snapshot. Only treat a filesystem write as confirmed when the application has a verifiable file handle or equivalent acknowledgment.
7. Runtime loading of third-party Office document parsers
Classification: BAD
Severity: High
Scope: Localized
The DOCX and XLSX import paths dynamically load executable parser libraries from:
unpkg for Mammoth

cdnjs for SheetJS

The relevant loader and import paths are in:
src/core/app.js:60958–60997

src/core/app.js:63757–63814

The loader validates the origin against an allowlist, but it does not set Subresource Integrity metadata and executes the downloaded script in the main Sutra origin.
There is no evidence that the normal libraries upload imported documents. The risk is a supply-chain boundary:
a compromised CDN response or dependency distribution can execute with full access to Sutra’s origin

that script can access the workspace, credentials exposed through same-origin APIs, and the document being parsed

offline DOCX/XLSX import fails even though core Sutra is positioned as local-first

the dependency behavior differs from vendored JSZip, PDF.js, and other locally controlled critical runtimes

Recommended direction: Vendor pinned, reviewed parser versions into the deploy artifact and service-worker manifest. A stronger design would run parsing in an isolated worker or sandbox with a narrow data bridge.
8. Trusted markup and inline-script debt remain too large
Classification: BAD
Severity: High for maintainability, Medium for direct security risk
Scope: Systemic
The central sanitizer is strong, but the guardrail baseline still permits a substantial legacy surface. The current baseline records hundreds of trusted or dynamic markup sinks in app.js and more across the repository.
Sutra.html also uses:
script-src 'unsafe-inline'

style-src 'unsafe-inline'

numerous inline handlers

numerous inline style attributes

a broad approved script and connection host list

These are not all exploitable vulnerabilities. Many sinks contain developer-authored templates that are routed through the trusted helper. The problem is the size of the trusted surface:
a reviewer must distinguish user-controlled content from static template fragments across hundreds of locations

CSP cannot act as a strong final script-injection barrier while unsafe-inline remains

one incorrect classification can bypass the central sanitizer

security review is dependent on repository-specific conventions and static baselines

Guardrails stop the count from increasing. They do not reduce the existing exposure.
9. Accessibility assurance is weaker than the visual QA posture
Classification: BAD
Severity: Medium
Scope: Cross-cutting
Sutra includes meaningful accessibility work:
skip links

dialog roles

modal focus management

:focus-visible styling

reduced-motion rules

forced-colors rules

mobile focus restoration

keyboard interaction tests

The broad accessibility test suite is much less stringent than its name suggests:
landmark coverage passes when any qualifying landmark exists

reduced-motion coverage ultimately asserts only that the result is a Boolean

200% zoom coverage checks that the body still has nonzero dimensions

small touch targets are logged but do not fail

accessible-name issues are logged but do not fail

several checks inspect only the first subset of elements

Static inspection also surfaced numerous form controls that warrant manual accessible-name verification, although some may receive names from runtime enhancement or nearby labels.
Impact: The suite can remain green while keyboard, screen-reader, touch-target, reflow, or contrast problems persist on less-traveled surfaces.
This is an assurance problem, not evidence that the whole product is inaccessible.
10. Weak tests dilute confidence from the strong ones
Classification: BAD
Severity: Medium
Scope: Recurring
Some chaos tests attempt to simulate meaningful failures but do not verify the intended invariant strongly enough. Examples include:
attaching a pageerror listener after the potentially failing reload

overriding an IndexedDB method in a way unlikely to intercept the actual transaction path

asserting only that the document body exists

performing rapid tab changes and then asserting a literal true value

allowing the DOM to grow to nearly three times its original size

starting an export, reloading, then only checking that some UI exists

Impact: These tests increase case count and execution time without proportionally increasing confidence.
Direction: Every chaos test should name and verify an invariant, such as:
exact data survives

no stale revision commits

warning state appears

rollback state remains available

no duplicate event fires

no unexpected network call occurs

active focus is restored

a measured resource count remains bounded

11. Manual load-order and cache-stamp coordination
Classification: BAD
Severity: Medium
Scope: Systemic
Feature development frequently requires coordinating:
a script path in Sutra.html

the correct classic-script load position

query-string cache stamps

asset-manifest entries

service-worker versions

guardrail scan lists

path-coupled checks

documentation

legacy global aliases

The feature documentation explicitly describes this move/edit burden.
The cache-stamp lock contains manual version strings and content hashes for a large portion of the source graph.
Impact: A correct source edit can still ship stale, be omitted from the offline artifact, collide in global scope, or fail because another path-based check was not updated.
This is build-system work being performed manually through convention.
12. Production response-header verification does not clearly follow the actual deployment target
Classification: BAD
Severity: Medium
Scope: Deployment boundary
vercel.json defines strong headers, including frame-ancestors 'none', nosniff, no-referrer, permissions restrictions, COOP, CORP, and HSTS.
The production-header checker validates vercel.json by default and only checks a real HTTPS deployment when a URL is supplied.
The deployment workflow inspected deploys to GitHub Pages and runs a live smoke test, but it does not visibly run the live header checker against that deployed Pages URL.
Therefore, the repository proves that the intended headers exist in Vercel configuration. It does not prove in the checked pipeline that equivalent headers are present on the actual GitHub Pages deployment.
This matters especially for frame-ancestors, which must be delivered as a response header rather than relying on a meta CSP.
13. Silent failure remains a recurring implementation pattern
Classification: BAD
Severity: Medium
Scope: Systemic
The central reporter exists, but the global runtime contains many silent or minimally handled catches. Some are appropriate because browser capability detection and cosmetic cleanup should not break the product. Others appear in interaction, rendering, and lifecycle paths where a diagnostic breadcrumb would be useful.
Impact:
partially initialized features can look like empty states

broken controls may fail without explanation

production diagnostics can omit the original cause

tests may pass because the exception was swallowed

the same defensive catch pattern can conceal data-flow mistakes

The solution is not to surface every exception to the user. It is to make suppression explicit and observable.
Architecture Assessment
The architecture Sutra actually has
Sutra is not a conventional component application with an import graph. Its actual architecture consists of seven interacting layers.
1. Static application shell
Sutra.html owns:
the DOM skeleton

script ordering

stylesheet ordering

CSP meta policy

much of the initial view markup

global controls and overlays

It functions simultaneously as HTML template, dependency manifest, route shell, style-order definition, and startup configuration.
2. Global runtime aggregate
src/core/app.js owns the primary state object and many controllers. It communicates with feature scripts through top-level names and window.* bridges.
3. Organizational feature scripts
Feature directories improve repository navigation, but they are not hard module boundaries. The repository explicitly states that features communicate through globals rather than imports.
4. Persistence and safety services
These are the cleanest cross-cutting boundaries:
IndexedDB workspace storage

cross-tab coordination

safe secondary storage

migrations

DOM safety

error reporting

feature isolation

startup health

credential vault

5. Portable workspace model
A broad appData aggregate is serialized, migrated, exported, imported, backed up, and projected into Sync records.
6. Independent high-quality subsystems
Sync, cryptography, migrations, PDF engines, some academic engines, plugin validation, and selected Assistant components are substantially more modular and testable than the central runtime.
7. Layered CSS cascade
Styling is organized into folders, but runtime precedence is determined by <link> order and specificity rather than an enforceable layer graph.
What has scaled well
Static deployment remains operationally simple.

Local-first operation works without an account.

Compatibility identifiers preserve existing user data.

Pure modules can run in Node tests.

Cross-cutting safety services are available before feature boot.

The encrypted backup and Sync contracts remain independent of the UI implementation.

The system can run without a mandatory backend.

The deployed artifact is deterministic and testable.

What is starting to strain
The dependency graph exists primarily in human knowledge.

app.js closure dependencies prevent straightforward extraction.

Feature folders can imply separation that does not actually exist.

State ownership is broad and mutable.

Whole-workspace persistence makes unrelated domains participate in the same save lifecycle.

CSS ordering and script ordering are architectural constraints.

Cache invalidation is manually represented in source paths.

Many tests assert implementation shape because public module boundaries do not exist.

Hidden views and code remain eager.

Compatibility aliases and global APIs expand the integration surface.

Is the architecture still appropriate?
It is still capable of supporting the current product under disciplined maintenance and comprehensive regression testing.
It is not appropriate for another large wave of feature expansion without structural work.
A big-bang rewrite would create severe data and behavior risk. The correct strategy is a strangler-style decomposition:
Preserve the static output and storage contracts.

Define explicit runtime services.

Route new work through those services.

Extract pure state and domain logic first.

Move one view/controller at a time.

Stop adding new responsibilities to app.js.

Delete old bridges only after compatibility and migration coverage prove they are no longer needed.

Code Quality Assessment
Strong code quality
The best modules have several consistent traits:
narrow purpose

pure or injected dependencies

explicit validation

deterministic behavior

precise comments

clear failure semantics

bounded inputs

dual browser/Node execution where useful

tests that directly execute the public API

Sync crypto, Sync merge, migrations, workspace DB, plugin validation, and Assistant permissions fall into this group.
Weak code quality
The core runtime has the opposite characteristics:
mixed state, rendering, persistence, network, modal, editor, and product logic

thousands of functions in one file

closure-bound helpers

extensive DOM querying

global compatibility bridges

high event-listener density

numerous best-effort catches

broad mutation reach

little enforceable dependency direction

Largest code units
File
	Approximate size
	Approximate lines
	
src/core/app.js
	4.85 MB
	85,393
	
styles/base/styles.css
	1.01 MB
	35,316
	
Sutra.html
	649 KB
	8,916
	
src/features/assistant/flow-assistant.js
	532 KB
	8,581
	
styles/themes/sutra-pro.css
	197 KB
	6,860
	
These are beyond the point where naming, comments, and search alone can provide reliable modularity.
Duplication
The most consequential duplication is conceptual rather than literal copy-paste:
canonical workspace versus localStorage mirrors

global feature state versus appData

desktop shell versus mobile adapters

multiple representations of save, backup, and sync status

repeated modal and overlay patterns

repeated responsive override patterns

multiple deadline and upcoming summaries

multiple terminology sets for the same core surfaces

The mobile navigation correctly avoids duplicating routes. That pattern should be applied more broadly.
Naming and compatibility
Legacy names such as noteflow_atelier_db, flowAssistant, and .atelier formats should not be treated as careless naming. They intentionally preserve existing installations and third-party integration behavior.
The weakness is that legacy aliases remain part of the active dependency graph. They should be isolated behind compatibility adapters rather than used as ordinary internal vocabulary.
Comments and documentation
Documentation quality is high, but some comments are performing work that types, modules, interfaces, and dependency tooling would normally perform.
A long warning explaining why a function cannot move is useful. It is also evidence that the architecture cannot express the boundary mechanically.
Dead code
There is clearly substantial legacy and compatibility code. The audit did not establish that all of it is dead. Much of it is intentionally retained for old data, old URLs, old plugins, and old storage identifiers.
The right approach is not a mass deletion. It is:
instrument compatibility-path use

define sunset criteria

preserve import-only adapters separately

remove only paths proven unused and covered by migrations

Reliability and Data Integrity Assessment
Current confidence
Reliability is stronger than the codebase shape initially suggests.
The system has explicit defenses for:
failed IndexedDB reads

stale writes

blocked upgrades

cross-tab writes

accidental empty roots

lifecycle interruption

corrupted localStorage

missing attachments

incomplete backup packaging

import validation

migration failures

cloud conflicts

Sync conflicts

device revocation

account switching

partial cloud operations

Main strength
The save pipeline does not equate “transaction requested” with “data is safe.” It tracks confirmed saves and performs read-back checks.
That is the correct priority for a student workspace.
Main weakness
The persistence layer receives data from a very broad mutable runtime. Every additional guard compensates for an upstream architecture in which:
editors retain local state

feature modules retain globals

localStorage mirrors remain active

imports replace broad state

Sync applies remote projections

multiple tabs may edit

UI state and durable state are interleaved

This creates a reliability paradox:
Sutra has one of its strongest implementations around one of its most pressured architectural boundaries.

Homework source of truth
Keeping Homework’s live state in localStorage while mirroring it into appData was likely a compatibility decision. It works, and the module has defensive write and rollback behavior.
Long term, it remains a second source of truth. The canonical workspace should eventually own Homework, with localStorage retained only as a migration and compatibility mirror.
Attachments
Separating binary bytes from workspace metadata is sound. It avoids ballooning the primary root and allows content-addressed encrypted Sync.
It also creates referential-integrity obligations:
metadata without bytes

bytes without links

PDF pages referencing removed sources

backup completeness

Sync asset hydration

deletion across multiple contexts

Sutra addresses many of these correctly. This subsystem should remain explicit and transactional.
Import and restore
Validation, checksums, migrations, secret stripping, and delayed mutation are strong.
The automatic plaintext pre-import snapshot is the major exception. A recovery mechanism used to authorize destructive replacement must itself be both private and verifiably durable.
Reliability verdict
User data is better protected than the architecture rating might imply. The biggest future reliability gain will come not from adding another recovery layer, but from reducing the number of independent mutation and state paths.
Testing Assessment
Quantity
The repository has:
approximately 91 unit-test files

approximately 92 Playwright specification files

more than 500 unit-side cases

more than 500 browser-side cases

static checks for shell integrity, links, migrations, persistence, responsive behavior, CSP, headers, assets, guardrails, service workers, network policy, and deployment artifacts

browser projects across Chromium, Chrome, Firefox, WebKit, mobile Chromium, mobile WebKit, tablet, and narrow desktop

This is a serious verification investment.
Highest-quality testing
The strongest tests are found where the implementation offers a clean public boundary:
Sync protocol and merge

cryptography

migration behavior

account and device isolation

backup round-trip invariants

exact deploy artifact

modal focus behavior

cross-browser packaged-artifact testing

These tests make meaningful claims about state and output.
Lowest-quality testing
The weakest tests generally appear where the global runtime is difficult to isolate:
source-string checks presented alongside behavioral unit tests

VM extraction of implementation fragments

body-exists smoke assertions

log-only accessibility violations

fault injection that does not intercept the real production seam

stress tests without exact data assertions

loose DOM-growth bounds

tests that confirm a control is focusable but not that the workflow is keyboard-complete

Accessibility testing
The broad accessibility suite should become much stricter.
Recommended minimum gates:
axe-core or equivalent automated rules on each primary view

no unnamed interactive controls

complete keyboard path through navigation, modals, editors, and settings

focus restoration after every overlay

no focus entering inert backgrounds

200% and 400% reflow with no essential two-axis scrolling

reduced-motion behavior verified by computed animation and transition values

hard 44-pixel target checks for primary phone interactions

contrast validation across every shipped theme

screen-reader smoke testing on principal workflows

CI strategy
The exact-artifact release process is excellent. The main opportunity is to divide verification into clearer categories:
architecture and source-policy checks

executable unit tests

integration tests

browser user-flow tests

accessibility tests

performance budgets

provider-contract simulations

This would make the reported test counts more meaningful.
Testing verdict
The suite provides good confidence for persistence, Sync, backup, deployment, and selected core workflows. It provides less confidence than its size implies for general UI integrity, accessibility, lifecycle cleanup, and feature-level fault recovery.
Performance Assessment
Baseline concerns
The main performance problem is not one obviously inefficient loop. It is the accumulated baseline:
very large eager JavaScript graph

giant app.js

giant CSS cascade

thousands of initial DOM nodes

many hidden views

many listeners and observers

repeated global DOM queries

whole-workspace serialization and hashing

several advanced editors available in the same shell

limited true lazy loading

Likely bottlenecks
Startup
The browser must parse and compile a large body of JavaScript and CSS before the user interacts with advanced features that may never be opened.
Style calculation
A 69,000-line stylesheet system with heavy specificity and !important usage makes style matching and recalculation more expensive, especially with thousands of nodes.
Memory
Keeping many view trees, controller closures, event handlers, editor infrastructure, and feature globals alive raises baseline memory use.
Saving
Whole-workspace freezing, JSON serialization, hashing, comparisons, and read-back verification are sensible for integrity but become increasingly expensive as pages, versions, slides, sheets, Assistant histories, and metadata grow.
The debounce reduces frequency, not per-save cost.
Search and aggregation
Global search, deadline ranking, dashboards, Assistant context derivation, and Sync projections can become expensive if they repeatedly scan broad workspace collections without maintained indexes or incremental selectors.
Rich content
Slides, Sheets, Canvas, PDFs, page version history, and inline images can substantially increase workspace and DOM size. The repository already notes that Slides image data URLs can grow the workspace and should eventually move to the attachment store.
Existing mitigations
service-worker caching

versioned assets

attachment byte separation

debounced persistence

optional Assistant and Business loading

bounded histories in selected subsystems

sparse Sheet representation

Sync records and content-addressed assets

benchmark tooling

Benchmark concern
The heavy benchmark is separate from the default verification path, and its ceilings are generous enough to permit a noticeably slow student experience.
A product-level performance budget should measure:
first meaningful paint

time to usable Today

input latency on Notes

view-switch latency

save-confirmation latency

search latency at realistic large-workspace sizes

memory after visiting every core view

mobile long-task count

CSS and JS transferred, parsed, and executed

incremental growth after repeated view transitions

Performance verdict
Sutra is likely acceptable on a modern desktop with warm caches. It is increasingly vulnerable on older laptops, school Chromebooks, and phones.
The first major performance improvement should be loading and mounting less, not micro-optimizing individual helper functions.
Security and Privacy Assessment
Strong boundaries
Encrypted backups and Sync
The cryptographic primitives and envelope design are appropriate, and authentication metadata is bound through AES-GCM additional data.
User content sanitization
The allowlist sanitizer removes dangerous elements, blocks event handlers, validates URLs, and filters styles.
Credentials
The device credential vault uses AES-GCM, random IVs, a non-extractable key, atomic key creation, and guarded writes.
This provides useful protection against casual IndexedDB inspection and raw backup inclusion. It does not protect secrets from malicious same-origin code that can invoke the vault API, which makes XSS and external-script control especially important.
Plugins
The plugin sandbox is well designed for a browser-only local extension model.
Assistant
Context and actions are permissioned, sensitive areas have separate gates, and consequential changes require approval.
Service worker
It avoids caching provider traffic and user exports.
Privacy communication
The workspace lock accurately describes itself as a privacy screen rather than encryption.
Main concerns
1. Remote parser scripts
The DOCX/XLSX import path introduces avoidable same-origin supply-chain execution.
2. Plaintext pre-import snapshots
Automatic unencrypted workspace downloads conflict with the encrypted-backup default and cannot be fully verified through an anchor-click fallback.
3. CSP is not yet a strong containment boundary
The policy blocks many dangerous defaults, but unsafe-inline and approved external script origins reduce its value against script injection.
4. Large trusted HTML surface
The sanitizer boundary is strong, but there remain hundreds of locations where developer-authored HTML is trusted. One mistaken classification can expose user content.
5. Production header uncertainty
The intended response headers are strong, but equivalent enforcement on the actual GitHub Pages deployment is not established by the checked release workflow.
6. Broad provider surface
Sutra supports numerous AI providers, storage providers, OAuth systems, custom endpoints, Supabase projects, and embedding origins. Each expands CSP, credential, error, and privacy complexity.
The code makes meaningful attempts to bound these. The cumulative surface is still large.
Security verdict
Sutra’s security posture is better than that of a typical browser-only productivity prototype. It is not yet at the point where the browser origin can be treated as a tightly contained trusted computing base.
The most valuable next security work is not replacing the cryptography. It is:
removing optional remote executable parsers

eliminating automatic plaintext recovery files

reducing trusted markup sinks

externalizing inline scripts and handlers

verifying real deployment headers

minimizing the number of scripts executing in the main origin

UI Audit
Strongest UI qualities
Visual identity
Sutra has a recognizable identity rather than appearing to be a generic component library demo.
Hierarchy
Today generally answers “what matters next” before showing supporting detail.
Writing experience
Notes provides a convincing document environment with strong page focus and typography.
Homework
Homework presents courses, status, due dates, and deadlines clearly. Its table and filters are familiar enough to understand without training.
Timeline
Day and Week views communicate temporal structure effectively.
Testing Hub
The Testing Hub and Review views feel purpose-built rather than merely restyled task lists.
Assistant
The Assistant UI is polished and appropriately distinct without looking detached from Sutra.
Mobile Today
The mobile Today screen is one of the strongest adaptations in the product.
Weakest UI qualities
Repeated floating utility controls
Several screens accumulate right-edge floating buttons for feedback, fullscreen, Assistant, saving, and other actions. They compete with content and create a second informal navigation layer.
Excessive status repetition
Homework and dashboard views sometimes repeat the same information through summary cards, tabs, badges, side panels, and the main table.
Toolbar density
The Notes toolbar is powerful but long and icon-heavy. Less common operations compete visually with basic writing controls.
Settings density
Settings contains too many equally weighted decisions. It needs a clearer separation between common, advanced, experimental, and developer-like configuration.
Upcoming Radar legibility
The Radar’s visual novelty exceeds its information clarity.
Theme layering
Most principal surfaces are coherent, but advanced themes and feature-specific panels sometimes appear to apply a skin over controls that were not designed from the same component primitive.
UI verdict
The visual design is one of Sutra’s assets. The next phase should remove competing chrome, consolidate repeated summaries, and strengthen component ownership, not redesign the entire visual language.
UX Audit
The strongest mental model
Sutra is strongest when it behaves as one connected loop:
Capture something.

It becomes Homework, a Note, a reminder, or a time block.

Home identifies what matters.

Timeline schedules it.

Focus helps execute it.

Review converts it into active recall.

Save and backup status make the work trustworthy.

The repository’s current product direction explicitly identifies Home, Capture, Homework, Create, Timeline, Review, Focus, and Data/Backup as the intended center.
That direction is correct.
Where UX loses coherence
Competing organizational systems
A user can encounter:
tasks

Homework

assignments

milestones

deadlines

All Due

Timeline blocks

study sessions

Review items

Cram sessions

course work

custom dashboards

These are not identical data types, but the user-facing boundaries are not always obvious.
Competing creation surfaces
Notepad, Canvas, Slides, Sheets, HTML pages, PDFs, and imported Office documents are powerful. They increase the decision burden when a student simply wants to “make something.”
Advanced categories become separate products
College, Life, Business, AP Study, Testing Hub, Course Hub, and Assistant each have their own local information architecture.
Cloud terminology
The implementation’s distinctions leak into the UX. Users encounter several concepts that all sound like “my data is somewhere else.”
Terminology drift
Home versus Today and Create versus Notes are the most visible examples.
Context switching
The more a workflow requires moving among Home, Homework, Assignment Studio, Timeline, Focus, Notes, and Review, the more important deep links and state preservation become.
Sutra has built entity and action infrastructure to address this, but it needs to become the dominant interaction model.
Recoverability
Recoverability is a strong UX area:
save status is visible

backup status is visible

conflicts are explicit

destructive import has a safety step

failure banners provide recovery actions

workspace lock explains its limitations

cloud and Sync remain optional

The plaintext safety-snapshot issue should be fixed without losing this strong recoverability posture.
First-time versus advanced users
Sutra increasingly handles this through feature packs and default view selection. The next step is to treat advanced capability as contextually discoverable, not simply hidden in Settings.
Examples:
offer Assignment Studio when a large Homework item is created

offer Review generation from a Note or test

offer Timeline scheduling from a deadline

offer Slides or Sheets when a note’s purpose suggests them

offer College tools when the user enables the College pack

offer Assistant only after permissions and purpose are understood

UX verdict
The core daily workflow is viable and differentiated. The broader workspace feels like several capable applications sharing a shell.
Product coherence will improve more by connecting and consolidating existing actions than by adding new top-level capabilities.
Mobile and Responsive Audit
What works
Bottom navigation prioritizes the daily student loop.

Advanced sections remain accessible through one sheet.

Mobile navigation delegates to canonical routes.

Notes receives a drawer rather than permanently losing horizontal space.

Focus management and Back behavior are considered.

Safe-area spacing is present.

Gestures attempt to avoid editors and interactive controls.

Reduced motion affects vibration and transitions.

Timeline Month adapts rather than merely shrinking a desktop grid.

The mobile Today screenshot has strong hierarchy and appropriate control sizing.

What remains weak
Responsive architecture is highly override-driven
Hundreds of media queries and several breakpoint families indicate accumulated adaptation rather than a small set of intentional responsive primitives.
Advanced surfaces remain desktop-first
Sheets, large tables, College matrices, dense settings, PDF editing, and Week calendars inherently need more deliberate mobile modes.
Touch-target assurance is incomplete
The audit tooling warns at 32 pixels for general controls, while primary phone interactions should consistently meet the documented 44-pixel goal.
Mobile QA is not yet uniformly hard-gated
The dedicated mobile audit is useful, but it is separate and produces diagnostic output rather than acting as a standard release blocker.
Landscape and virtual keyboards
Complex editors need explicit tests for:
keyboard opening and closing

visual viewport resizing

selection toolbars

fixed bottom navigation

modal height

split panes

rotated devices

safe-area changes

Mobile verdict
The primary mobile shell is no longer prototype-grade. It is credible.
The complete application is not yet equally convincing on mobile. Mobile quality is highest for the daily loop and lower for advanced creation, administration, and data-heavy surfaces.
Consistency Audit
Positive consistency
The visual language is recognizable across major views.

Mobile navigation reuses desktop route ownership.

Modal accessibility has shared infrastructure.

Save, Sync, and backup status are increasingly separated.

The entity registry is intended to create common open/action semantics.

Encryption and permission boundaries follow repeatable patterns.

Design tokens exist and are widely used.

Advanced packs do not delete data when hidden.

Inconsistent terminology
Today versus Home

Notes versus Create

Review versus Review & Tests versus Testing Hub

Cram Hub as both an older destination and a consolidated redirect

Cloud Backup versus Drive Sync versus Sutra Sync

legacy Flow/Atelier names within current bridges

Inconsistent state handling
canonical IndexedDB workspace

Homework localStorage source

device-local preference stores

Assistant history migration mirrors

attachment databases

credential database

Sync operational database

temporary share database

feature-owned runtime globals

These are not all inappropriate, but they do not all follow one mutation and observation model.
Inconsistent UI composition
shared modal manager versus custom overlays

shared tokens versus feature-specific hardcoded values

standard page headers versus floating actions

dense dashboard cards versus document-focused whitespace

settings controls versus custom feature configuration panels

Inconsistent architectural patterns
pure dual-mode modules

classic global IIFEs

giant global script

lazy manifest features

eagerly linked feature scripts

source-extracted tests

directly imported Node-testable modules

Sutra already contains examples of the architecture it should move toward. The inconsistency comes from incomplete migration, not absence of a viable direction.
Technical Debt Map
Debt category
	Level
	Assessment
	
app.js ownership and global runtime
	Structural
	The central source of change amplification and isolation difficulty.
	
State mutation and persistence coupling
	Structural
	Too many mutators, mirrors, globals, and lifecycle paths feed one workspace aggregate.
	
Eager shell and view mounting
	Structural
	Performance and memory costs are paid for features users may never open.
	
CSS cascade and specificity
	Structural
	Load order, legacy overrides, and !important are architectural constraints.
	
Product information architecture
	Significant
	Daily-loop coherence competes with many advanced centers of gravity.
	
Plaintext pre-import fallback
	Significant
	Privacy mismatch and unverifiable rollback guarantee.
	
Remote Office parser execution
	Significant
	Avoidable main-origin supply-chain exposure.
	
Trusted HTML and inline CSP debt
	Significant
	Large audit surface and weak final containment.
	
Test signal consistency
	Significant
	Strong critical-path tests coexist with low-value checks.
	
Accessibility assurance
	Significant
	Good foundations, insufficient hard enforcement.
	
Manual script order and cache stamps
	Significant
	Correctness depends on coordinated editing across several manifests and files.
	
Cloud-product mental model
	Moderate
	Technically valid systems are difficult to distinguish as outcomes.
	
Error suppression
	Moderate
	Too many best-effort catches lack explicit classification.
	
Legacy compatibility aliases
	Moderate
	Necessary today, but should be isolated rather than remain normal dependencies.
	
Advanced mobile surfaces
	Moderate
	Primary mobile paths are strong; complex workspaces lag.
	
Documentation drift and stale line references
	Low
	Documentation is generally strong; occasional details lag rapid code growth.
	
Cosmetic naming remnants
	Low
	Mostly harmless when not exposed to users.
	
Highest-Leverage Improvements
1. Establish an explicit runtime boundary around app.js
Problem: The global runtime owns too many unrelated responsibilities.
Recommended direction: Introduce explicit services such as a workspace store, persistence service, command layer, view router, modal service, attachment service, and integration boundary. New features should depend on these interfaces rather than directly reaching into closure state or arbitrary globals.
Extract pure normalizers, selectors, validators, and domain commands first. Move one complete vertical slice at a time.
Expected impact: Major improvement in maintainability, testability, dependency clarity, and regression isolation.
Scope: Architectural
2. Route durable changes through a canonical command and transaction layer
Problem: Hundreds of call sites can mutate state and trigger persistence through different paths.
Recommended direction: Define commands such as:
create or update Homework

move page

update note content

schedule item

mark complete

apply import

apply remote projection

update settings

Each command should validate, mutate canonical state, increment revision, emit domain events, and schedule persistence through one route.
Expected impact: Fewer stale writes, fewer forgotten persistence triggers, clearer audit trails, easier undo, and simpler Sync integration.
Scope: Architectural
3. Make advanced surfaces genuinely lazy and mountable
Problem: Navigation hides features without removing much of their startup cost.
Recommended direction: Extend the feature registry to College, Life, Course Hub, AP Study, Testing Hub, PDF, Slides, Sheets, custom dashboards, and other advanced areas. Load code and CSS on first use, and mount or unmount view DOM intentionally.
Expected impact: Faster startup, lower memory, fewer global listeners, smaller style surface, and clearer feature boundaries.
Scope: Large
4. Replace plaintext pre-import snapshots
Problem: Full restores can create unencrypted workspace JSON and proceed based on an unverifiable browser download.
Recommended direction: Make the internal previous-root journal the primary rollback guarantee. When an external snapshot is necessary, generate an encrypted .sutra file. Only claim external durability when a filesystem write or comparable operation can be confirmed.
Expected impact: Better privacy, more truthful recovery guarantees, and alignment with the encrypted-backup model.
Scope: Medium
5. Vendor or isolate Office parsers
Problem: DOCX and XLSX parsing loads third-party code into the primary origin at runtime.
Recommended direction: Vendor pinned parser versions in the deploy artifact, include them in integrity and service-worker checks, and preferably run parsing in a worker or sandbox with a narrow message interface.
Expected impact: Reduced supply-chain risk, reliable offline import, and stronger local-first consistency.
Scope: Medium
6. Rebuild the CSS ownership model incrementally
Problem: The cascade relies on file order, large legacy layers, and thousands of !important declarations.
Recommended direction:
adopt explicit cascade layers

define a small breakpoint vocabulary

identify component primitives

scope feature CSS to feature roots

migrate one legacy block at a time

ratchet !important counts downward

test themes through shared component fixtures

avoid introducing a new global style for a local feature problem

Expected impact: More predictable UI changes, fewer regressions, easier theme support, and lower responsive complexity.
Scope: Large
7. Convert source-shape tests into executable boundary tests
Problem: Many tests protect implementation text rather than behavior.
Recommended direction: Keep source checks as explicitly named architecture checks. Expose pure or injected modules from the runtime and test them through public APIs. Rewrite weak chaos tests around precise state and failure invariants.
Expected impact: Higher confidence per test, less brittleness during extraction, and faster architectural evolution.
Scope: Large
8. Turn accessibility into a release gate
Problem: Several broad accessibility violations are logged but do not fail verification.
Recommended direction: Add hard automated checks for accessible names, keyboard completion, focus containment, reflow, reduced motion, contrast, and touch targets across principal views and themes.
Expected impact: More reliable keyboard and assistive-technology support, fewer late regressions, and better mobile usability.
Scope: Large
9. Reduce trusted markup and tighten CSP
Problem: Hundreds of trusted HTML sinks and inline script requirements prevent CSP from acting as a strong containment layer.
Recommended direction: Prioritize sinks that combine templates with variable content, replace inline handlers with delegated listeners, externalize inline scripts, move static templates into safe builders or template elements, and progressively remove unsafe-inline.
Run the production-header checker against the actual deployment URL.
Expected impact: Smaller XSS audit surface, stronger defense in depth, and simpler security review.
Scope: Large
10. Consolidate product information architecture
Problem: Advanced features increasingly operate as separate applications.
Recommended direction: Organize around the daily-loop outcomes:
Plan

Create

Learn

Focus

Reflect

Protect data

Use contextual actions to reveal advanced features. Standardize Home/Today and Create/Notes terminology. Remove duplicate summaries and competing deadline presentations.
Expected impact: Lower cognitive load, better discoverability, clearer onboarding, and stronger product identity.
Scope: Large
11. Add enforceable performance budgets
Problem: Performance tooling exists, but the default release process does not strongly bound startup, interaction, memory, or payload growth.
Recommended direction: Gate:
critical JS and CSS bytes

time to usable Home

Notes input responsiveness

view-switch time

save-confirmation latency

mobile long tasks

DOM count

listener and observer growth after navigation cycles

large-workspace search and Sync projection times

Expected impact: Prevents gradual regression and makes architectural extraction visibly valuable.
Scope: Medium
12. Automate dependency and cache manifests
Problem: Manual query stamps and load ordering create avoidable coordination cost.
Recommended direction: Generate content-hashed asset references and manifests from a build-time graph while preserving static output. Treat the generated deployment folder as the public app.
Expected impact: Fewer stale deployments, less merge conflict pressure, simpler feature moves, and a more enforceable dependency graph.
Scope: Medium
Things I Would NOT Change
1. Do not abandon local-first operation
Mandatory accounts or a server-first workspace would remove one of Sutra’s clearest differentiators and introduce a different class of privacy and availability risk.
2. Do not replace the persistence engine casually
The atomic write, stale-write protection, recovery root, confirmed marker, startup block, and read-back verification should be treated as critical infrastructure.
3. Do not perform a big-bang framework rewrite
A wholesale rewrite would endanger backup compatibility, migrations, editor behavior, imported content, Sync semantics, and years of edge-case hardening.
Modernize through bounded seams.
4. Do not rename legacy storage identifiers without migration
Names such as noteflow_atelier_db are compatibility contracts. Cosmetic cleanliness is not worth user-data loss.
5. Do not simplify Sync into last-write-wins
The deterministic conflict model is one of Sutra’s strongest technical decisions.
6. Do not weaken attachment completeness checks
A backup that silently omits required bytes is worse than a refused backup.
7. Do not replace encrypted .sutra with ordinary JSON as the default
JSON should remain an explicit advanced recovery format.
8. Do not remove exact-artifact deployment verification
Build once, test once, and deploy the tested bytes.
9. Do not create a second mobile routing system
Continue delegating through canonical navigation.
10. Do not discard the existing visual identity
The interface needs consolidation, not generic redesign.
11. Do not remove advanced features solely to make screenshots look simpler
Progressive disclosure, contextual entry points, and workflow consolidation are preferable to deleting mature capabilities without evidence.
12. Do not weaken Assistant approval and permission boundaries
The Assistant should continue proposing consequential changes rather than silently applying them.
13. Do not weaken the plugin sandbox
Local plugins should remain isolated, permissioned, disabled on import, and network-restricted.
14. Do not confuse adding build tooling with abandoning static deployment
Sutra can use modules, generated manifests, type checking, bundling, or code splitting while still publishing a static offline-capable application.
Final Verdict
How healthy is the codebase?
Moderately healthy overall, but sharply uneven.
It is healthy in:
data safety

recovery

encryption

migrations

Sync

release engineering

offline behavior

critical-path documentation

visual design

It is unhealthy in:
central runtime size

dependency clarity

CSS ownership

state mutation discipline

eager loading

broad maintainability

accessibility assurance

product scope control

Is the architecture still appropriate for Sutra’s current size?
It can continue operating at its current size because the repository has extensive guardrails and knowledgeable maintenance practices.
It is no longer an appropriate foundation for substantial feature expansion without decomposition.
What will become painful as Sutra grows?
adding a persistent field

changing editor behavior

modifying navigation

altering a shared component

adding another cloud or provider path

maintaining mobile parity

preserving every theme

reasoning about save timing

preventing listener and DOM accumulation

keeping cache stamps and manifests aligned

distinguishing old compatibility code from active code

testing one feature without booting nearly everything else

Does the product feel cohesive?
The daily student loop feels cohesive.
The entire product feels partially consolidated. College, Life, Business, advanced academic tools, document editors, Assistant, customization, and cloud systems still behave too much like capable subproducts attached to one shell.
Which parts feel production-grade?
canonical workspace persistence

encrypted .sutra backups

migration and portability discipline

Sutra Sync protocol and crypto

service-worker update behavior

exact-artifact release pipeline

plugin sandbox

Assistant permission boundary

core Today, Notes, Homework, Timeline, and Assistant visual treatment

modal accessibility infrastructure

storage-health and recovery communication

Which parts still feel prototype-grade?
the 85,000-line global runtime

the implicit script dependency graph

eager loading of most product surfaces

the global CSS cascade

widespread trusted markup

inline handler dependence

some chaos and accessibility tests

advanced mobile surfaces

duplicate summaries and terminology

the number of distinct top-level product concepts

automatic plaintext pre-import snapshots

runtime CDN loading for document parsers

Largest risks
Change amplification in the global runtime.

State and persistence complexity across many mutation paths.

Performance and memory growth from eager loading.

CSS regressions from specificity and override debt.

Product incoherence from continued scope expansion.

Privacy and supply-chain inconsistencies around import workflows.

Accessibility problems escaping because broad checks are soft.

A future engineer weakening safety behavior while attempting a large cleanup.

What would concern an experienced engineer inheriting Sutra?
The first concern would be that apparently local changes are not actually local. They would need to understand load order, globals, CSS order, storage compatibility, cache stamps, manifests, feature bridges, import/export, Sync portability, and tests before touching foundational behavior.
The second concern would be the gap between repository organization and actual runtime boundaries. Files look grouped, but many boundaries are conventions rather than enforced interfaces.
The third concern would be the amount of product surface expected to remain simultaneously polished, responsive, accessible, portable, and synchronized.
What would impress them?
They would likely be impressed by:
the seriousness of the local persistence system

the deterministic encrypted Sync design

the fail-closed attachment and backup behavior

the migration and portability inventory

the exact-artifact release pipeline

the plugin isolation model

the honesty of privacy disclosures

the breadth of test and static-check infrastructure

the quality of the core UI

the fact that the repository documents its architectural landmines rather than pretending they do not exist

GOOD: Data safety, encrypted backups, deterministic Sync, migration discipline, exact-artifact deployment, plugin isolation, Assistant permissions, service-worker behavior, core visual design, and the mobile daily loop.
MID: Static deployment, progressive disclosure, onboarding, Settings, mobile breadth, cloud concepts, error-handling adoption, and overall test quality.
BAD: The 85,000-line global runtime, uncontrolled mutation reach, eager payload and DOM, structural CSS debt, product scope sprawl, plaintext pre-import snapshots, remote Office parser execution, trusted-markup debt, soft accessibility enforcement, and manual load-order/cache coordination.
Biggest strength: Sutra treats user data, encryption, recovery, and Sync with unusual seriousness.
Biggest weakness: The application’s composition has not kept pace with the sophistication and breadth of the product built inside it.
Most important next investment: Incrementally establish a real runtime and state boundary around app.js, then use that boundary to make advanced features lazy, transactional, independently testable, and easier to consolidate into one coherent student workflow.
